commands.name: awk
commands.description: awk splits each input record into fields, tests its pattern, and runs the associated action. NR is the record number, $0 the whole record, and $1… the fields; -F chooses the field separator.

anatomy.label: PROGRAM
anatomy.text: A pattern-action program. A pattern selects records; `{ action }` runs only for selected records. `BEGIN` and `END` handle setup and summaries.

anatomy.label: Fields
anatomy.text: `$0` is the whole record, `$1` and `$2` are fields, `NF` is the field count, and `NR` is the record number.

anatomy.label: Options and files
anatomy.text: `-F` sets the field separator; `-v name=value` passes a value into the program before it begins. File operands supply records. This is not a CSV parser when quoted fields can contain delimiters.

anatomy.label: Output and external effects
anatomy.text: `print > path` writes records to a file and may replace its prior contents. `system()` starts a shell command; never concatenate untrusted field data into that command. Validate names and values before using them as paths or commands.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Alfred V. Aho, Peter J. Weinberger, and Brian W. Kernighan designed and implemented the original Unix awk.

origins.label: When
origins.text: The original implementation was written in 1977; the language was later expanded in 1985 and standardized through POSIX.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: AT&T Bell Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: They wanted a small pattern-action language for scanning records and fields, making common report generation and data transformation concise without writing a full program in C.

cases.title: Use Case 01: Print usernames and home directories
cases.what: Reads the local account database and displays each account name beside its home-directory field.
parts: -F':' sets the input field separator to a literal colon.
$1 and $6 refer to the username and home-directory fields in this colon-delimited format.
The action prints the two selected fields separated by awk’s output field separator.

cases.title: Use Case 02: Select records containing an error word
cases.what: Filters a text log to show records containing the case-sensitive word ERROR.
parts: /ERROR/ is a regular-expression pattern applied to the complete record.
With no explicit action, awk prints each record whose pattern matches.

cases.title: Use Case 03: Align two columns with printf
cases.what: Formats the first two whitespace-separated fields as left-aligned columns.
parts: printf uses the supplied format string instead of adding a newline automatically.
%-15s left-aligns a string in a field at least 15 characters wide; the second %s does the same for field two.
\n ends each output row; $1 and $2 supply the two values.

cases.title: Use Case 04: Print one record by its number
cases.what: Displays the tenth input record for a focused inspection.
parts: NR == 10 selects the tenth record in the input stream.
print $0 emits the complete selected record; awk does not number records in the file itself.

cases.title: Use Case 05: Print a bounded record range
cases.what: Shows records 20 through 30 inclusive without loading a separate range tool.
parts: NR == 20 starts the address range.
The comma keeps the rule active through the first record where NR == 30.
With no action, each record in the active range is printed.

cases.title: Use Case 06: Find records with an unexpected field count
cases.what: Lists whitespace-delimited records that do not have exactly four fields.
parts: NF is awk’s count of fields in the current record.
!= 4 selects records whose field count differs from four; the default action prints each selected record.

cases.title: Use Case 07: Print the last field without knowing its position
cases.what: Extracts the final whitespace-delimited field from every record.
parts: $ introduces a field reference.
NF evaluates to the number of fields, so $NF refers to the final field in the current record.

cases.title: Use Case 08: Find lines longer than a style limit
cases.what: Prints records whose character length exceeds 80, helping review long source lines.
parts: length($0) measures the current full record.
The pattern is true only when the measured length is greater than 80; the default action prints that record.

cases.title: Use Case 09: Add a report heading before processing
cases.what: Prints one heading before listing the first field from each input record.
parts: BEGIN runs once before awk reads records.
The second action runs once per record and prints field one.
Use a sample or approved input when displaying account-related data.

cases.title: Use Case 10: Report how many records were read
cases.what: Prints the final record count after the input stream has been processed.
parts: END runs once after the last input record.
NR retains the total record number reached; an empty file leaves it at zero.

cases.title: Use Case 11: Sum a numeric column
cases.what: Adds the numeric values in field two and prints the total at end of input.
parts: sum += $2 adds field two to an accumulator for every record.
END prints the final accumulator after input is complete.
The example assumes the field contains numeric data and no header row.

cases.title: Use Case 12: Calculate an average with an empty-input guard
cases.command: awk '{sum += $3; count++} END {if (count) print "Average:", sum/count}' metrics.txt
cases.what: Computes the mean of numeric values in field three without dividing by zero on empty input.
parts: The per-record action accumulates field three and increments count.
END runs after the records; if count is nonzero, sum/count computes the mean.
Skip or validate a header row if the file has one.

cases.title: Use Case 13: Combine exact and numeric conditions
cases.what: Selects rows for the named account whose third field exceeds 50, then displays field two.
parts: $1 == "root" compares field one to the exact string root.
&& requires both tests to be true.
$3 > 50 performs a numeric comparison; the sample file must define what its fields mean.

cases.title: Use Case 14: Match an email domain suffix
cases.what: Prints records whose second field ends in the literal suffix .org.
parts: $2 selects the second field.
~ applies a regular-expression match.
\. matches a literal period and $ anchors the pattern at the end of that field.

cases.title: Use Case 15: Exclude successful HTTP status codes
cases.what: Shows sample log records whose third field does not begin with a 2xx status code.
parts: !~ is the regular-expression nonmatch operator.
^ anchors the pattern at the start of field three; 2 followed by two digits describes a 2xx prefix.
Confirm the sample log’s field layout before relying on this filter.

cases.title: Use Case 16: Rebuild whitespace-delimited fields as CSV-like output
cases.what: Joins the fields of each whitespace-delimited record with commas for simple data inspection.
parts: BEGIN sets OFS, the separator used when awk rebuilds output fields.
Assigning $1 to itself marks the record as changed; print then joins fields with the new OFS.
This is not a CSV parser and does not quote commas inside values.

cases.title: Use Case 17: Track a maximum while reading records
cases.command: awk 'NR == 1 || $4 > max {max=$4; label=$1} END {if (NR) print "Maximum:", max, label}' response.sample
cases.what: Finds the largest numeric value in field four and reports the associated label from field one.
parts: NR == 1 initializes max from the first record, including when later values are negative.
Later records replace max and label only when $4 is larger.
END reports the result only when at least one record was read.

cases.title: Use Case 18: Select odd-numbered records
cases.what: Prints records 1, 3, 5, and so on.
parts: NR % 2 calculates the remainder after division by two.
A remainder of one selects odd record numbers; the default action prints them.

cases.title: Use Case 19: Split records on a literal double-pipe delimiter
cases.what: Reads records separated by a space, two literal vertical bars, and another space.
parts: -F supplies the input field-separator regular expression.
The backslashes make each vertical bar literal instead of regex alternation.
The two print expressions select the fields on either side; awk’s OFS separates them in output.

cases.title: Use Case 20: Label a record using a conditional
cases.what: Adds a simple label based on whether the numeric value in field two exceeds 90.
parts: if evaluates the comparison $2 > 90 for each record.
The true branch prints field one with CRITICAL; else handles all other values with OK.
Confirm that field two is numeric before interpreting the threshold.

cases.title: Use Case 21: Keep the first copy of each full record
cases.what: Removes repeated complete lines while keeping the order of each line’s first appearance.
parts: seen[$0] uses the full record as an associative-array key.
Post-increment returns the previous value, which is zero the first time and nonzero later.
The leading ! makes only the first occurrence true, so awk prints it by default.

cases.title: Use Case 22: Aggregate bytes by client address
cases.command: awk '{bytes[$1] += $2} END {for (ip in bytes) print ip, bytes[ip]}' access.sample
cases.what: Totals field two separately for each distinct address in field one.
parts: bytes[$1] indexes an associative array by the first field and accumulates the second field.
The END loop visits each key once after reading all records.
Array iteration order is unspecified; pipe through sort when stable order matters.

cases.title: Use Case 23: Count records by status value
cases.command: awk '{count[$3]++} END {for (status in count) print status, count[status]}' access.sample
cases.what: Builds a frequency count for each value in field three.
parts: count[$3] selects a counter keyed by the current third field.
The END loop prints each key and its count.
The output order is unspecified unless sorted.

cases.title: Use Case 24: Join two files by a shared key
cases.command: awk 'FILENAME == ARGV[1] {value[$1]=$2; next} $1 in value {print $0, value[$1]}' labels.txt records.txt
cases.what: Adds the matching description from the first file to records in the second file.
parts: FILENAME == ARGV[1] identifies records from the first named input, even when it is empty.
value[$1]=$2 stores the first file’s description by key; next skips the remaining rules for that record.
$1 in value selects second-file records with a known key.
This holds the first file’s keys in memory and assumes both files use the same key in field one.

cases.title: Use Case 25: Extract a fixed-width substring
cases.what: Reads five characters beginning at character position ten in each record.
parts: substr takes the source string, a one-based starting position, and a maximum length.
Here $0 is the full record, 10 is the starting position, and 5 is the requested length.

cases.title: Use Case 26: Search without case sensitivity
cases.what: Matches warning text regardless of letter case and prints the full record.
parts: tolower($0) converts the record to lowercase for comparison.
~ tests the converted string against /warning/.
The action prints the original record, preserving its original letter case.

cases.title: Use Case 27: Replace hyphens in one field
cases.what: Replaces every hyphen in field one with an underscore and prints the updated record.
parts: gsub takes a regular expression, replacement string, and target field.
The target $1 limits changes to the first field.
Changing a field rebuilds $0 and can normalize spacing using OFS.

cases.title: Use Case 28: Split a date field and select its month
cases.what: Extracts the middle component of a YYYY-MM-DD value in field two.
parts: split copies field two into the array parts using a hyphen separator.
AWK arrays use one-based string or numeric subscripts; parts[2] is the month component.
Check for malformed or missing date fields when processing untrusted input.

cases.title: Use Case 29: Reverse the field order in each record
cases.command: awk '{for (i=NF; i>0; i--) printf "%s%s", $i, (i==1 ? ORS : OFS)}' text.txt
cases.what: Prints each record’s fields from last to first with standard output separators.
parts: The loop starts at NF and decrements until it reaches one.
$i selects the field at the current loop index.
The conditional prints ORS after the final field and OFS between earlier fields, avoiding a trailing separator.

cases.title: Use Case 30: Match one of several exact port values
cases.what: Selects records whose fourth field is exactly one of the listed port numbers.
parts: $4 selects the port field.
^ and $ anchor the match to the complete field, preventing 18080 from matching 8080.
(80|443|8080) lists the accepted alternatives.

cases.title: Use Case 31: Pass a shell value as an awk variable
cases.what: Selects account records whose first field matches the current shell user.
parts: The shell expands the quoted USER value before awk starts.
-v assigns that value to awk variable target before the program runs.
The quoted program compares field one to target; for arbitrary values containing backslashes or newlines, use a carefully designed data channel instead.

cases.title: Use Case 32: Warn about filesystems above a threshold
cases.command: df -P | awk 'NR > 1 {used=$5; sub(/%$/, "", used); if (used+0 > 90) print $1, used "%"}'
cases.what: Reports filesystem rows above 90 percent used without turning the result into a kill or cleanup action.
parts: df -P requests a predictable one-line-per-filesystem layout on systems that support it.
NR > 1 skips the header; $5 is copied so sub can remove its trailing percent sign.
used+0 forces numeric comparison; the action reports the filesystem and percentage for review.

cases.title: Use Case 33: Pass selected fields safely to a shell loop
cases.command: awk '$5+0 > 90 {print $1}' usage.sample | while IFS= read -r filesystem; do printf 'Review: %s\n' "$filesystem"; done
cases.what: Shows how awk can select records for a shell loop that prints a review reminder.
parts: $5+0 compares a numeric usage field to 90.
awk emits only the selected filesystem field.
The quoted read loop preserves whitespace in each line; this example reports candidates and does not alter storage.

cases.title: Use Case 34: Return a failure status when a fatal record appears
cases.what: Returns status 1 if any record contains FATAL and zero otherwise, allowing a caller to branch on the result.
parts: /FATAL/ selects matching records and sets found.
END runs once after input; the conditional exit expression returns 1 when a match was seen.
This scans the complete input, so it can report a final status consistently.

cases.title: Use Case 35: Write validated categories to separate lab files
cases.what: Routes records to files named for a restricted category value inside a lab output directory.
parts: The regular expression allowlist rejects slashes and unexpected filename characters in field three.
path combines a fixed lab directory and the validated value.
> opens or truncates that output file; close releases it after each record. Create and inspect the lab directory first.

cases.title: Use Case 36: Format constrained values as JSON lines
cases.what: Formats an allowlisted name and integer as a JSON object per record; arbitrary text needs a JSON encoder.
parts: The two regular expressions restrict the name and numeric field to values that need no JSON escaping.
printf inserts the fields into a fixed JSON template and ends each object with a newline.
For general strings, use a JSON serializer such as jq rather than hand-built escaping.

cases.title: Use Case 37: Resolve validated hostnames in a shell loop
cases.command: awk '$1 ~ /^[A-Za-z0-9.-]+$/ {print $1}' hosts.txt | while IFS= read -r host; do nslookup "$host"; done
cases.what: Looks up hostname-shaped values one at a time without building a shell command from raw file contents.
parts: The awk regular expression restricts the candidate hostname characters.
The pipe sends one candidate per line to the loop.
Quoted "$host" is one argument to nslookup; review the host list and use only authorized DNS queries.

cases.title: Use Case 38: Measure change between adjacent values
cases.what: Prints the difference between the current second-field value and the preceding record.
parts: NR > 1 skips the first record because it has no predecessor.
The first action subtracts the saved previous value from the current field.
The second action updates previous on every record for the next iteration.

cases.title: Use Case 39: Read blank-line-separated paragraphs
cases.what: Treats blank-line-separated blocks as records and selects blocks whose first line names TargetServer.
parts: RS set to the empty string enables paragraph-style records in common awk implementations.
FS set to newline makes each line within a paragraph a field.
$1 tests the first line; verify local awk behavior and the file’s block format.

cases.title: Use Case 40: Use a terminal width with a default
cases.what: Passes the shell’s COLUMNS value to awk, falling back to 80 when it is unset or empty.
parts: ${COLUMNS:-80} is shell parameter expansion performed before awk starts.
-v assigns the resulting value to width.
BEGIN prints it once; this example reports a setting but does not itself align a table.

cases.title: Use Case 41: Apply a percentage adjustment after a header
cases.what: Raises numeric values in field three by ten percent while leaving the first header record unchanged.
parts: NR == 1 prints the header and next skips the later action for that record.
For subsequent records, $3 *= 1.10 updates field three.
print emits the updated record; it writes to standard output and leaves the source file unchanged.

cases.title: Use Case 42: Select records between two markers
cases.what: Prints a range beginning with the first START_BLOCK record and ending with the next END_BLOCK record.
parts: /START_BLOCK/ opens the range.
The comma is awk’s range-pattern operator.
/END_BLOCK/ closes the active range after that record, which is included in output.

cases.title: Use Case 43: Count categories in sorted key order
cases.command: awk '{count[$1]++} END {for (key in count) print key, count[key]}' data.txt | sort
cases.what: Counts field-one values and sorts the resulting key-count rows for stable display.
parts: count[$1]++ increments an associative-array counter.
The END loop emits one row per key; awk does not promise an array iteration order.
sort orders the emitted rows alphabetically by their first field.

cases.title: Use Case 44: Trim surrounding spaces from a field
cases.what: Removes leading and trailing spaces or tabs from field one and prints that cleaned value.
parts: The regular expression alternation matches leading whitespace or trailing whitespace.
gsub replaces every matching run with an empty string in field one only.
print emits the cleaned field; locale and awk implementation can affect character handling.

cases.title: Use Case 45: Keep unique two-field pairs
cases.what: Prints the first record for each distinct combination of fields one and two.
parts: The comma in an awk array subscript joins fields with SUBSEP to form a composite key.
The post-increment is zero on a new pair and nonzero on later repetitions.
The leading ! selects only first occurrences, preserving input order.

cases.title: Use Case 46: Find non-ASCII bytes in a controlled text file
cases.what: Under the C locale, reports records containing bytes outside printable ASCII, except horizontal tab.
parts: LC_ALL=C sets byte-oriented character classification for this command.
The bracket expression accepts tab and printable ASCII space through tilde; its negation selects other bytes.
This is a byte-level diagnostic, not a Unicode validator; use an encoding-aware tool for UTF-8 correctness.

cases.title: Use Case 47: Filter categories after aggregation
cases.command: awk '{count[$1]++} END {for (key in count) if (count[key] > 500) print key, count[key]}' access.sample
cases.what: Prints only keys that occur more than 500 times in the input.
parts: The main action counts records by field one.
The END loop examines completed totals.
The condition is applied after aggregation, like a HAVING filter; output order remains unspecified.

cases.title: Use Case 48: Format epoch seconds with GNU awk
cases.what: Converts a numeric epoch-seconds field to a readable local date and prints it beside field two.
parts: gawk identifies GNU awk, whose strftime function is an extension rather than a POSIX awk guarantee.
The format string requests year, month, day, hour, minute, and second.
$1 supplies epoch seconds; local timezone settings affect the displayed time.

cases.title: Use Case 49: Report the source file and record number
cases.what: Shows each input filename, its per-file record number, and the complete record.
parts: FILENAME is the current input path.
FNR starts again at one for each file, unlike NR which counts across all files.
The shell expands the quoted-free wildcard before awk starts; unmatched glob behavior depends on the shell.

cases.title: Use Case 50: Find a term in any field and report its position
cases.command: awk '{for (i=1; i<=NF; i++) if ($i ~ /CRITICAL/) print "Line", FNR, "field", i, $i}' system.log
cases.what: Checks every whitespace-separated field and reports the record and field position for matches.
parts: The loop visits each field index from one through NF.
$i refers to the field at the current index.
The regular expression tests for CRITICAL within that field; FNR reports its position in the current file.

cases.title: Use Case 51: Print every input record
cases.what: Print every input record.
parts: With no pattern, the action runs for every record.
`print` with no expressions emits the whole record, much like cat for a small text file.

cases.title: Use Case 52: Select comma-separated fields
cases.what: Select comma-separated fields.
parts: `-F,` sets the input field separator to a comma.
This handles simple rows only; quoted CSV fields containing commas require a CSV parser.

cases.title: Use Case 53: Split on commas, spaces, or tabs
cases.what: Split on commas, spaces, or tabs.
parts: `-F` accepts a regular expression here: a run of commas, spaces, or tabs separates fields.
The quotes keep the shell from interpreting the expression.

cases.title: Use Case 54: Pass a shell value into the program
cases.what: Pass a shell value into the program.
parts: The shell expands the quoted variable into one argument; `-v` assigns it to awk’s `limit` variable before the program runs.

cases.title: Use Case 55: Select records matching a pattern
cases.what: Select records matching a pattern.
parts: A regular-expression pattern with no action uses awk’s default action, which prints each matching record.

cases.title: Use Case 56: Match a pattern in one field
cases.what: Match a pattern in one field.
parts: `$2 ~ /^A/` tests whether field two begins with A; `$0` prints the entire matching record.

cases.title: Use Case 57: Require an exact field value
cases.what: Require an exact field value.
parts: `==` compares field three with the exact string.
This is equality, not a substring search.

cases.title: Use Case 58: Filter a numeric range
cases.what: Filter a numeric range.
parts: `&&` requires both inclusive bounds, selecting status values from 400 through 499.

cases.title: Use Case 59: Print one record number
cases.what: Print one record number.
parts: `NR` is the current record number across the input stream.
With no explicit action, matching records are printed.

cases.title: Use Case 60: Print an inclusive record range
cases.what: Print an inclusive record range.
parts: The comma range starts at record five and remains active through record ten, including both endpoints.

cases.title: Use Case 61: Add report boundaries
cases.command: awk 'BEGIN {print "--- REPORT START ---"} {print $1} END {print "--- END ---"}' data.txt
cases.what: Add report boundaries.
parts: `BEGIN` runs before input, the unpatterned action runs once per record, and `END` runs after the final record.

cases.title: Use Case 62: Set input and output separators
cases.what: Set input and output separators.
parts: `FS` splits each input record at colons; `OFS` joins the two printed fields with an arrow.
Use a sample file rather than exposing real account data.

cases.title: Use Case 63: Choose output from an if/else branch
cases.what: Choose output from an if/else branch.
parts: The condition is evaluated for each record; the selected branch labels the first field according to the numeric threshold.

cases.title: Use Case 64: Sum a numeric column
cases.what: Sum a numeric column.
parts: Uninitialized numeric variables start at zero.
This assumes field three contains valid numbers and has no header row.

cases.title: Use Case 65: Find the maximum value and its label
cases.command: awk 'NR == 1 || $3 > max {max = $3; route = $1} END {print "Max:", max, "on route", route}' data.txt
cases.what: Find the maximum value and its label.
parts: The first record initializes the maximum; later records replace it only when field three is larger.
Input must contain numeric values in that field.

cases.title: Use Case 66: Count error records
cases.what: Count error records.
parts: The pattern counts records whose third field is exactly ERROR.
`count+0` prints zero when no record matched.

cases.title: Use Case 67: Take a substring from a field
cases.what: Take a substring from a field.
parts: `substr` uses one-based positions and returns up to four characters from field one.

cases.title: Use Case 68: Replace text in one field
cases.what: Replace text in one field.
parts: `gsub` replaces every match in field two.
Assigning a field rebuilds `$0` using `OFS`, so original spacing between fields may change.

cases.title: Use Case 69: Find lines beyond a width
cases.what: Find lines beyond a width.
parts: `length($0)` measures the record; `NR` reports its position.
Character counting can depend on awk implementation and locale.

cases.title: Use Case 70: Aggregate values by category
cases.command: awk '{sales[$1] += $2} END {for (item in sales) print item, sales[item]}' business.txt
cases.what: Aggregate values by category.
parts: ` sales` is an associative array keyed by the first field.
Iteration order is unspecified; sort the output if stable order matters.

cases.title: Use Case 71: Count distinct client addresses
cases.command: awk '{ip_counts[$1]++} END {for (ip in ip_counts) print ip, ip_counts[ip]}' access.log
cases.what: Count distinct client addresses.
parts: Each first-field value becomes an array key.
The result order is unspecified, and field one must actually be the address in this log format.

cases.title: Use Case 72: Keep the first record for each key
cases.what: Keep the first record for each key.
parts: The first occurrence sees a zero counter and is printed; later records with that key are suppressed.
Input order is preserved.

cases.title: Use Case 73: Validate names before preparing directories
cases.what: Validate names before preparing directories.
parts: The allowlist rejects slashes and shell metacharacters before producing candidate paths.
Review the list before passing it to a separate directory-creation step; avoid `system()` on untrusted fields.

cases.title: Use Case 74: Write records to validated per-category files
cases.what: Write records to validated per-category files.
parts: The allowlist prevents a category value from supplying path separators; `close` releases each output file handle.
Create the output directory first and treat this as a write operation.

cases.title: Use Case 75: Report the largest numeric field
cases.what: Report the largest numeric field.
parts: The guard accepts integer values only; the pipeline sorts the report and limits display to ten rows.

cases.title: Use Case 76: Count events by level
cases.command: awk '{count[$3]++} END {for (level in count) print level, count[level]}' app.log
cases.what: Count events by level.
parts: Associative-array keys group records by field three; sort the output when deterministic order matters.

cases.title: Use Case 77: UID Range Intelligence
cases.what: UID Range Intelligence.
parts: `>` sends standard output to the named file and truncates an existing file first.

cases.title: Use Case 78: UID Range Intelligence
cases.what: UID Range Intelligence.
parts: `>` sends standard output to the named file and truncates an existing file first.

cases.title: Use Case 79: 10.7 Tool Building: The Practical Engineer
cases.what: 10.7 Tool Building: The Practical Engineer.
parts: `>` sends standard output to the named file and truncates an existing file first.

commands.name: bash
commands.description: bash starts a Bash shell or interprets a script. A script can execute every command available to its user; inspect it before running and use `bash -n` only as a syntax check, not as a safety check.

anatomy.label: [OPTION…]
anatomy.text: Options select output, filtering, or operation details; check this implementation’s help because flags vary by program.

anatomy.label: [ARGUMENT…]
anatomy.text: Operands supply the paths, names, records, or values the command acts on. Confirm the target and the expected output before a state-changing invocation.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Brian Fox wrote Bash for the GNU Project; Chet Ramey later became its maintainer and a major contributor.

origins.label: When
origins.text: The GNU Project reported Bash complete in June 1988; later public beta milestones followed. The cited contemporary bulletin establishes the 1988 milestone, not the exact start date.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: Created for the GNU Project by an FSF employee; the contemporary GNU announcement identifies the project and author but does not establish a development city.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: GNU needed a free, Bourne-shell-compatible command interpreter so its operating system could run shell scripts and support interactive and programmed use.

commands.name: cat
commands.description: cat copies each named file to standard output in order; with no file operand it reads standard input. It does not interpret a file as a document or safely edit it.

anatomy.label: [FILE…]
anatomy.text: Files are copied to standard output in order. With no files, cat reads standard input.

anatomy.label: When to choose a pager
anatomy.text: Use `less` for a large file; cat emits the entire input and is best for short files or deliberate stream composition.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: The First Edition manual does not name an individual author for `cat`. The manual credits Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie; the modern GNU implementation credits Torbjörn Granlund and Richard M. Stallman.

origins.label: When
origins.text: Attested in the First Edition Unix Programmer's Manual dated November 3, 1971; this documents its presence by that date rather than proving the exact day it was written.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: Research Unix at Bell Telephone Laboratories, running on the PDP-11/20 by the time the First Edition manual was prepared.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: To copy input streams and concatenate files in order, making it easy to inspect text or connect small tools through standard input and output.

commands.name: cd
commands.description: cd is a shell builtin because changing directory must change the current shell process. A child program cannot change its parent shell’s working directory. A relative operand is resolved from the current directory; ~ and directory variables may be expanded by the shell.

anatomy.label: [DIRECTORY]
anatomy.text: The destination for the current shell. A relative path starts from the current directory; `~`, `..`, and `-` refer to home, parent, and previous directory.

anatomy.label: Why it is built in
anatomy.text: A child process cannot change its parent shell’s working directory, so cd must run inside the shell that owns the session.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: The Bash project credits Brian Fox as its original author; this operation is part of the Bash shell rather than a separately created executable.

origins.label: When
origins.text: Bash development began in 1988; the exact first year of this individual builtin is not established by the cited manual.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: The GNU Bash project; its manual does not establish a city for this builtin's original implementation.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: Provide the shell operation `cd` as part of command interpretation, state, or session management.

commands.name: chmod
commands.description: chmod changes permission bits or ACL-related mode representation for the named path. Symbolic forms such as u+x modify one class and permission; recursive changes multiply the scope and deserve a preview.

anatomy.label: MODE
anatomy.text: Symbolic forms such as `u+x` change one class and permission; octal modes replace the complete permission set.

anatomy.label: FILE…
anatomy.text: Every named path is changed. Avoid broad recursive changes until a preview establishes the exact target set.

anatomy.label: Directory modes
anatomy.text: On a directory, `r` permits listing names and `x` permits traversal/search. Files and directories often need different modes, so do not apply one recursive mode blindly.

anatomy.label: Special bits and umask
anatomy.text: Setuid, setgid, and sticky bits are separate mode bits with security consequences. When `who` is omitted in symbolic notation, umask can affect which classes are changed; write `u`, `g`, `o`, or `a` explicitly when intent matters.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: The First Edition manual does not credit an individual implementer for `chmod`. The GNU Coreutils implementation credits David MacKenzie and Jim Meyering.

origins.label: When
origins.text: Attested in the First Edition Unix Programmer's Manual dated November 3, 1971; the exact initial coding date is not recorded there.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: The early Research Unix system at Bell Telephone Laboratories; GNU Coreutils is a later collaborative implementation.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: To change the access mode of a filesystem entry so its owner or an authorized administrator can control read, write, and execute permissions.

cases.title: Use Case 01: Add execute permission for the owner
cases.what: Add execute permission for the owner.
parts: The symbolic mode changes only the owner execute bit; the explicit path and -- keep the target unambiguous.
cases.note: This invocation changes the named file or its metadata; verify the lab path first.

cases.title: Use Case 02: Remove group write permission
cases.what: Remove group write permission.
parts: The symbolic mode removes the group write bit without replacing other permission bits.

cases.title: Use Case 03: Set others to read only
cases.what: Set others to read only.
parts: The equals operator sets the selected class exactly, so this clears write and execute for others.

cases.title: Use Case 04: Set every class to read and write
cases.what: Set every class to read and write.
parts: The `a` selector applies to owner, group, and others; `=` clears execute while setting read and write.

cases.title: Use Case 05: Combine independent symbolic clauses
cases.what: Combine independent symbolic clauses.
parts: The comma applies both clauses to the same file: add owner execute and set others to read only.
Keep the mode together without spaces.
cases.note: This invocation changes the named file or its metadata; verify the lab path first.

cases.title: Use Case 06: Add group read/write and remove other execute
cases.what: Add group read/write and remove other execute.
parts: The first clause adds two group bits; the second removes only execute for others.

cases.title: Use Case 07: Clear the permissions for others
cases.what: Clear the permissions for others.
parts: An empty permission list after `o=` clears that class; owner and group receive the exact sets shown.

cases.title: Use Case 08: Set different access for each class
cases.what: Set different access for each class.
parts: Comma-separated clauses set owner, group, and other permissions exactly; the `=` operator replaces the selected class’s bits.

cases.title: Use Case 09: Set a precise octal mode
cases.what: Set a precise octal mode.
parts: The digits are owner, group, others: 7 is 4+2+1 (`rwx`), 6 is 4+2 (`rw-`), and 4 is `r--`.
Octal notation replaces the mode.

cases.title: Use Case 10: Set a private configuration mode
cases.what: Set a private configuration mode.
parts: Owner read/write and group read are allowed; other users receive no access.
Verify ownership and required service identity too.

cases.title: Use Case 11: Add execute permission for the owner
cases.what: Adds the owner execute bit while preserving the other mode bits.
parts: `u` selects the owner class, `+` adds, and `x` selects execute.
`--` ends option parsing; the lab path scopes the change.

cases.title: Use Case 12: Set a private regular-file mode
cases.what: Allows the owner to read and write while clearing group and other access.
parts: 6 is read plus write; 0 grants no listed permission.
This is a common restrictive mode, but ownership and parent-directory permissions still matter.

cases.title: Use Case 13: Set a conventional readable file mode
cases.what: Gives the owner read/write access and gives group and others read access.
parts: 6 means read/write for the owner; each 4 means read only.
Use only when the file is intended to be readable by those classes.

cases.title: Use Case 14: Remove write access from every class
cases.what: Clears write permission for owner, group, and others while preserving their other mode bits.
parts: `a` selects all three permission classes.
Read-only mode bits do not prevent the owner from changing permissions again or guarantee immutability.

cases.title: Use Case 15: Copy owner permissions to the group
cases.what: Sets the group permission bits to match the owner bits.
parts: `g=u` uses the right-hand class as the source mode.
The group membership and directory path still determine who can reach the file.

cases.title: Use Case 16: Find world-writable files before repair
cases.what: Lists regular files with the others-write bit set for review.
parts: `-perm -0002` matches when the specified permission bit is present on common GNU/BSD find implementations.
This is an audit only; review each path and its purpose before changing modes.

cases.title: Use Case 17: Set private modes on SSH lab files
cases.what: Restricts the lab SSH directory to its owner and makes the sample configuration owner-readable/writable only.
parts: The first command needs directory traversal permission for its owner.
The second mode applies to the named file; actual SSH checks can differ by client and platform.

cases.title: Use Case 18: Restrict a sample authentication log
cases.what: Allows the owner to read/write, the group to read, and other users no access.
parts: 6 is owner read/write, 4 is group read, and 0 is no others permission.
Ownership must assign the intended group for this mode to serve its purpose.

cases.title: Use Case 19: Build a lab directory with deliberate ownership and mode
cases.what: Creates a lab directory, assigns its owner and group, then grants full access to those classes and read/traverse access to others.
parts: `&&` runs each step only if the preceding step succeeds.
Replace the account/group placeholders with existing identities; chown may require authorization.
775 permits group members to write, so confirm the group membership and intended sharing.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 20: Recognize why mode 777 is unsafe
cases.what: Demonstrates a mode that grants read, write, and execute to every class; use it only in a disposable lab.
parts: Each 7 means read, write, and execute.
World-writable access can allow other local users to alter content; choose the narrowest needed mode.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 21: Give a directory traversal and listing access
cases.what: Sets the owner to full access and grants group/others read plus directory traversal.
parts: For directories, `x` permits traversal/search; `r` permits listing names.
The same 755 mode is usually too broad as a blanket setting for every regular file.

cases.title: Use Case 22: Set web-tree directory and file modes separately
cases.command: find ./lab/web -type d -exec chmod 755 -- {} +; find ./lab/web -type f -exec chmod 644 -- {} +
cases.what: Applies one mode to directories and another to regular files under a lab web tree.
parts: The first find selects directories; the second selects regular files.
`-exec … {} +` safely batches paths. Inspect the tree and ownership before applying to a real deployment.

cases.title: Use Case 23: Preview executable scripts before changing them
cases.what: Lists candidate shell scripts so you can review the scope before adding execute bits.
parts: `-type f` excludes directories and `-name` matches the basename.
This is the read-only preview; run a scoped chmod only after confirming every listed path.

cases.title: Use Case 24: Add execute permission to reviewed scripts
cases.what: Adds execute permission for the owning user to reviewed shell scripts in a bounded tree.
parts: The search root limits scope.
`u+x` changes only the owner execute bit; it does not grant group or other execution.

cases.title: Use Case 25: Copy a mode from a reference file (GNU chmod)
cases.what: Copies the reference file’s permission mode to the target using GNU chmod.
parts: `--reference` is a GNU Coreutils extension.
The operation changes the target mode; confirm the reference and target before running.

cases.title: Use Case 26: Add the sticky bit to a shared lab directory
cases.what: Sets the sticky bit on a shared directory so users generally cannot remove or rename entries owned by others.
parts: `+t` adds the sticky bit.
It does not make the contents private or stop owners and privileged users from changing their files.

cases.title: Use Case 27: Add group inheritance to a collaboration directory
cases.what: Sets the setgid bit on a directory so new entries commonly inherit the directory group.
parts: `g+s` selects the group set-ID bit.
Exact inheritance behavior depends on the filesystem and operating system; verify the resulting owner and group.

cases.title: Use Case 28: Clear a special permission bit
cases.what: Removes the setuid bit from a reviewed lab file.
parts: `u-s` clears the user set-ID bit.
Setuid programs can run with the file owner’s identity; inspect ownership and package policy before changing system binaries.

cases.title: Use Case 29: Clear setgid from a collaboration directory
cases.what: Removes the directory’s setgid bit so newly created entries no longer receive its group-inheritance behavior where that behavior is supported.
parts: `g-s` removes the group set-ID bit.
Check existing files and the local filesystem behavior before changing a shared directory.

cases.title: Use Case 30: Inspect permissions before changing them
cases.what: Shows current mode, owner, group, and path for the targets.
parts: `-l` displays metadata and `-d` reports a directory itself rather than listing its contents.
Use this read-only check to confirm the intended target before chmod or chown.

commands.name: chown
commands.description: chown changes the owner and optionally the group of filesystem paths. Changing ownership usually requires administrative authority; recursive changes and symlink handling vary by implementation, so inspect the exact target and local manual first.

anatomy.label: OWNER[:GROUP]
anatomy.text: Names the new owner and optional group. An empty user before `:GROUP` changes only the group; a trailing colon can request the named user’s primary group, subject to implementation behavior.

anatomy.label: FILE…
anatomy.text: Changes ownership metadata for each path. Changing an owner usually requires administrative authority; an unprivileged owner may change a file only to a permitted group.

anatomy.label: Recursive and reference options
anatomy.text: `-R` descends through a tree and can affect many files; list the target set first. GNU `--reference=PATH` copies owner and group from a reference file.

anatomy.label: Symbolic links
anatomy.text: Follow-versus-act-on-link behavior and `-h` support vary by platform. Inspect the link and target with `ls -l` or `readlink` before changing ownership.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: The First Edition manual does not credit an individual implementer for `chown`. The GNU Coreutils implementation credits David MacKenzie and Jim Meyering.

origins.label: When
origins.text: Attested in the First Edition Unix Programmer's Manual dated November 3, 1971; the exact initial coding date is not recorded there.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: The early Research Unix system at Bell Telephone Laboratories; GNU Coreutils is a later collaborative implementation.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: To assign a file or directory to a user and, where specified, a group, supporting ownership and shared administration on a multi-user system.

cases.title: Use Case 01: Change a file owner (authorized account required)
cases.what: Changes the owner of a lab file to the named account.
parts: Replace `USER` with an existing account.
Changing ownership usually requires root or an authorized capability; changing owner may clear setuid/setgid bits.

cases.title: Use Case 02: Change only the group owner
cases.what: Keeps the current user owner and assigns the named group.
parts: The leading colon leaves the user portion empty.
The caller must be permitted to assign that group; replace `GROUP` with an existing group.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 03: Change user and group together
cases.what: Assigns both the specified owner and group to one path.
parts: The colon separates user and group names.
Confirm both names and the path first; ownership changes require suitable privilege.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 04: Copy ownership from a reference (GNU chown)
cases.what: Copies the owner and group from a reference path using GNU chown.
parts: `--reference` is a GNU Coreutils extension.
The target’s ownership changes; verify both paths before running.

cases.title: Use Case 05: Use a numeric user ID
cases.what: Assigns the file to UID 501 on systems where that identifier exists.
parts: A number is interpreted as an account ID when it maps to a user.
UID mappings differ across hosts; inspect with `id` before using numeric IDs.

cases.title: Use Case 06: Use a numeric group ID
cases.what: Assigns group ID 7002 while preserving the current owner.
parts: The colon selects group-only assignment.
Check that the GID exists and is the intended shared group.

cases.title: Use Case 07: Set owner and its primary group
cases.what: Changes the owner and requests that owner’s primary group.
parts: A trailing colon with an empty group asks implementations to use the user’s login group.
Confirm the resulting group with `ls -l` or `stat`; behavior and account databases vary.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 08: Report only actual ownership changes
cases.what: Prints a message when an ownership change occurs.
parts: `-c` means changes-only reporting in GNU and common implementations.
It still changes ownership when needed and requires appropriate privilege.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 09: Report every checked ownership operation
cases.what: Prints a verbose status line for the requested ownership operation.
parts: `-v` enables verbose reporting.
A success message does not replace checking the resulting metadata.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 10: Suppress most ownership error messages (GNU chown)
cases.what: Suppresses most error diagnostics while attempting the requested change.
parts: `-f` is force/silent behavior in GNU chown.
Use sparingly: hidden errors make failed or skipped changes harder to detect.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 11: Preview orphaned files before repair
cases.what: Lists regular files whose numeric owner has no matching account.
parts: `-nouser` is a find predicate for an unmapped owner.
Review each path before deciding who should own it; do not automatically assign all orphaned files to root.

cases.title: Use Case 12: Preview files with an unmapped group
cases.what: Lists regular files whose group ID has no matching group name.
parts: `-nogroup` tests group database resolution.
Choose the correct destination group for the data instead of applying a blanket repair.

cases.title: Use Case 13: Assign a reviewed set of files to a service account
cases.what: Assigns reviewed sample data files to a service identity and group.
parts: The search pattern and root bound the target set.
Substitute existing account/group names; ownership changes generally require authorization.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 14: Change group ownership throughout a team lab tree
cases.what: Changes the group owner recursively while preserving each path’s user owner.
parts: `-R` descends through the tree and can affect many files.
List and review `./lab/team-data` first; use a narrow target and verified group.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 15: Change both owner and group in a reviewed service tree
cases.what: Assigns every path under the bounded lab tree to the selected service account and group.
parts: `-R` applies to descendants and can make large changes.
Replace both names with verified accounts, preview the target tree, and confirm the service actually needs ownership.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 16: Keep recursive ownership within the intended root (GNU chown)
cases.what: Recursively changes the group for the lab tree while GNU chown retains its safeguard against treating `/` as the recursion root.
parts: `--preserve-root` is a GNU safeguard and is normally the default for recursive chown.
The explicit `./lab` target keeps this example bounded; never substitute `/` casually.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 17: Change ownership of a symlink itself (platform-specific)
cases.what: Requests that chown act on the symbolic link rather than follow it on implementations that support `-h`.
parts: `-h` behavior and availability differ between GNU and BSD/macOS implementations.
Inspect the link and target first; use the local manual before applying this option.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 18: Change the target reached through a symbolic link
cases.what: On common Unix implementations, chown follows the symbolic link and changes its target’s ownership.
parts: The target may be outside the apparent directory.
Inspect with `ls -l` and `readlink` before changing ownership; do not assume link metadata is changed.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

cases.title: Use Case 19: Apply ownership to a reviewed set from a shell array (Bash)
cases.command: files=(./lab/config.sample ./lab/data.sample); for file in "${files[@]}"; do chown -- USER:GROUP "$file"; done
cases.what: Runs the ownership change once per explicitly listed pathname.
parts: Bash arrays preserve spaces in filenames when expanded as `"${files[@]}"`.
Replace the account names and paths; authorization is required and each operation changes metadata.
cases.note: This changes permissions or ownership. Confirm the exact paths, identities, and required access before running; recursive changes magnify mistakes.

commands.name: curl
commands.description: curl makes a client request to a URL. Its flags control method, output, error handling, and timeouts; a successful transfer is not proof that the response is semantically correct.

anatomy.label: URL…
anatomy.text: The remote endpoint. Review scheme, host, port, redirects, and the destination before sending data or trusting a response.

anatomy.label: Request and body
anatomy.text: GET is the default. `--data` and `-F` send request bodies; `-X` changes the method label but does not construct a valid body by itself. PUT, PATCH, and DELETE can change server state.

anatomy.label: Output and diagnostics
anatomy.text: `-o FILE` chooses a local output path, `-O` uses the remote filename, `-i` includes headers, `-I` sends HEAD, and `-w` prints selected transfer metadata.

anatomy.label: Safety and portability
anatomy.text: Use timeouts, preserve TLS verification, protect credential files, and verify HTTP status separately from transfer success. Protocol support such as HTTP/2, HTTP/3, and newer options depends on the curl build.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Daniel Stenberg extended Rafael Sagula’s `HttpGet` utility; the project became a community effort.

origins.label: When
origins.text: Stenberg’s first release with his additions was December 17, 1996; the name `curl` arrived in 1998.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: The project’s primary history describes an Internet Relay Chat use case but does not establish a more precise city for the initial work.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: Stenberg wanted an IRC bot to retrieve currency-exchange data from websites automatically. The command grew into a general client for transferring data across protocols.

commands.name: cut
commands.description: cut selects byte, character, or delimiter-separated fields from each line. It does not parse quoted CSV fields, so use a CSV-aware tool when commas can occur inside quotes.

anatomy.label: Selection mode
anatomy.text: Choose bytes with `-b`, characters with `-c`, or delimiter-separated fields with `-d` and `-f`.

anatomy.label: Input limits
anatomy.text: cut works on simple line formats; it does not honor quoted delimiters in CSV. Use a CSV-aware parser for structured data.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Gottfried W. R. Luderer wrote the original Bell Labs cut; the GNU Coreutils version credits David M. Ihnat, David MacKenzie, and Jim Meyering.

origins.label: When
origins.text: First appeared in AT&T System III Unix in 1982; the GNU implementation followed later.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: The original utility was developed at AT&T Bell Laboratories; the GNU implementation is a distributed Free Software Foundation project.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: It provided a direct way to select fixed-position bytes or characters and delimiter-separated fields from each line, avoiding a script for routine column extraction. It is line-oriented and does not parse quoted CSV.

commands.name: file
commands.description: file identifies data by examining content signatures and structure, not merely the filename extension. Its answer is a useful clue, not a security verdict.

anatomy.text: Options select output, filtering, or operation details; check this implementation’s help because flags vary by program.

anatomy.label: [ARGUMENT…]
anatomy.text: Operands supply the paths, names, records, or values the command acts on. Confirm the target and the expected output before a state-changing invocation.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: A file-identification command existed in Research Unix; Ian Darwin wrote the widely used System V-derived implementation, with later substantial work by John Gilmore and other contributors.

origins.label: When
origins.text: Documented in Research Unix Fourth Edition in November 1973; Darwin's implementation followed later, with the exact first coding year not established by its manual.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: The early command belongs to Bell Laboratories Research Unix; Darwin's implementation location is not stated in the manual.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: The utility examines file contents to identify a likely format, including files whose names or extensions are missing or misleading.

commands.name: find
commands.description: find walks the named starting path and evaluates each test from left to right. Tests narrow the matches; actions such as -print or -exec decide what happens to them.

anatomy.label: [path…]
anatomy.text: The roots to walk: `.` starts here; `/var/log` searches one system area. Multiple roots can be supplied.

anatomy.label: [expression/criteria]
anatomy.text: Tests narrow the result set. `-name`, `-type`, `-mtime`, and `-size` inspect names or metadata. Adjacent tests are combined; group alternatives with escaped parentheses.

anatomy.label: [action]
anatomy.text: The default action is `-print`. `-exec TOOL {} +` passes matched paths as arguments in batches; `{}` marks each path and `+` ends the batch.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Dick Haight

origins.label: When
origins.text: Unix Version 5, 1974.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: Bell Laboratories, as part of the Programmer’s Workbench work.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: To walk directory trees and select files by conditions, replacing hand-built lists of path names with repeatable searches.

commands.name: git
commands.description: git commands operate on the repository at the current directory or a parent. Inspect status and diffs first: a displayed change may belong to the user, not the current task.

anatomy.label: COMMAND
anatomy.text: A subcommand such as `status`, `diff`, `show`, or `log` selects the repository operation.

anatomy.label: Repository state
anatomy.text: Check `git status` and inspect diffs before modifying or staging. Existing user edits are evidence to preserve, not disposable noise.

anatomy.label: Agent boundary
anatomy.text: Treat untracked and staged changes as separate state; never assume the whole worktree belongs to the agent.

origins.label: Creator(s)

origins.label: Where
origins.text: Created for Linux kernel development; the cited project history does not identify a city.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: To provide a fast, simple, distributed version-control system capable of supporting large projects and many parallel branches.

commands.name: grep
commands.description: grep selects lines whose text matches PATTERN. -E changes the pattern language to extended regular expressions, so alternation uses | and grouping uses parentheses without backslashes.

anatomy.label: PATTERN
anatomy.text: The text or regular expression tested against each input line. Single quotes prevent the shell from interpreting characters such as `|`, `*`, or `$`.

anatomy.label: [FILE…]
anatomy.text: Files to inspect; with no file, grep reads standard input, which lets it follow a pipe.

anatomy.label: Options
anatomy.text: `-E` enables extended regular expressions, `-F` treats the pattern literally, `-n` shows line numbers, `-i` ignores case, and `-l` prints names without matched content.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Ken Thompson extracted regular-expression matching from the ed editor at Doug McIlroy's request; McIlroy's account describes the initial use case.

origins.label: When
origins.text: In use by the Fourth Edition Unix manual of 1973; the date printed in the man-page header is not treated as a verified creation date.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: Bell Telephone Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: It let McIlroy search dictionary text for words matching phonetic rules without repeatedly opening and scanning each file in an editor. Its composable line-search role later became a model for Unix tools.

cases.title: Use Case 61: Basic text pattern matching inside a file
cases.what: Searches a file line-by-line and outputs every row containing the exact word "ERROR".

system.log : The target file to be scanned.

cases.title: Use Case 62: Case-insensitive pattern lookup
cases.what: Finds lines containing variations of the word "success", such as "SUCCESS", "Success", or "SuCcEsS".
parts: -i : Option flag that disables case sensitivity during processing.

cases.title: Use Case 63: Inverting the match logic to find non-matching lines
cases.what: Filters a log file to display only the lines that do NOT contain the word "DEBUG".
parts: -v : Inverts the matching logic, selecting non-matching lines.

cases.title: Use Case 64: Counting the total number of matching occurrences
cases.what: Outputs a single integer indicating how many times the word "FATAL" appears in the file.
parts: -c : Suppresses line output and returns a cumulative count of matched rows.

cases.title: Use Case 65: Displaying line numbers along with matching rows
cases.what: Prefixes each output line with its original 1-based line number from the file.
parts: -n : Displays the relative file line number directly before the matched text.

cases.title: Use Case 66: Matching exact whole words only
cases.what: Matches lines containing the discrete word "port", while ignoring longer words like "portal" or "ports".
parts: -w : Enforces word-boundary constraints around the search pattern.

cases.title: Use Case 67: Matching lines that match an exact whole string
cases.what: Selects a line only if its entire content matches the string "status=active" from start to finish.
parts: -x : Enforces a strict whole-line match constraint.

cases.title: Use Case 68: Listing only the names of files containing a match
cases.what: Scans multiple python scripts and prints only the filenames where the word "TODO" is found.
parts: -l : Suppresses regular text output and prints only matching filenames.

cases.title: Use Case 69: Listing filenames that do NOT contain a match
cases.what: Scans script files and identifies which ones are missing the word "License".
parts: -L : Lists only the filenames of records that fail to match the query pattern.

cases.title: Use Case 70: Limiting the absolute volume of output lines
cases.what: Stops scanning a file after finding and displaying the first 5 matching instances.
parts: -m 5 : Maximum count flag that terminates line processing once the threshold is reached.

cases.title: Use Case 71: Printing trailing context lines after a match
cases.what: Prints the line containing "Exception" along with the 3 lines directly following it.
parts: -A 3 : "After" context flag. Outputs 3 trailing rows after a successful match.

cases.title: Use Case 72: Printing leading context lines before a match
cases.what: Prints the line containing "CRASH" along with the 2 lines directly preceding it.
parts: -B 2 : "Before" context flag. Outputs 2 leading rows ahead of a successful match.

cases.title: Use Case 73: Printing surrounding context lines around a match
cases.what: Displays a complete window of 2 lines before and 2 lines after any row containing "TIMEOUT".
parts: -C 2 : "Context" flag. Uniformly prints lines directly above and below the matched entry.

cases.title: Use Case 74: Recursive directory searching
cases.what: Traverses a folder and all its subfolders to find every file containing the string "DB_PASSWORD".
parts: -r : Recursively reads all files under each directory.

cases.title: Use Case 75: Recursive searching following symbolic links
cases.what: Recursively searches directories while following symlinks encountered along the file tree path.
parts: -R : Extended recursive flag that follows all symbolic link shortcuts.

cases.title: Use Case 76: Filtering files by inclusion patterns during recursive lookups
cases.what: Recursively searches the /etc directory, but only checks files ending with ".conf".
parts: --include=...: Limits the recursive search to filenames matching the specified glob pattern.

cases.title: Use Case 77: Excluding specific filenames during recursive lookups
cases.what: Searches a directory for "api_key", skipping minified JavaScript source files.
parts: --exclude=...: Skips files that match the specified glob pattern.

cases.title: Use Case 78: Excluding entire directories from a recursive search
cases.what: Searches a workspace while skipping heavy or irrelevant folders like node_modules and .git.
parts: --exclude-dir: Prevents the specified directories from being processed.

cases.title: Use Case 79: Sourcing search patterns directly from a reference file
cases.what: Uses every line in bad_ips.txt as a separate search pattern to query firewall.log.
parts: -f : Reads newline-separated search patterns from the specified file.

cases.title: Use Case 80: Suppressing error messages about missing or unreadable files
cases.what: Searches files without displaying terminal warnings if a file does not exist or lacks read permissions.
parts: -s : Silent mode flag. Suppresses error messages about unreadable or missing files.

cases.title: Use Case 81: Utilizing Extended Regular Expressions (ERE)
cases.what: Finds lines containing either "unauthorized" OR "forbidden" using extended regex syntax.
parts: -E : Activates Extended Regular Expression support (interprets character tokens like '|' without escaping).

cases.title: Use Case 82: Isolating only the exact matched text segment
cases.what: Extracts and outputs only the "id=XXXX" segment, rather than printing the entire log line.
parts: -o : Outputs only the exact non-empty parts of a matching line, with each part on a separate line.

cases.title: Use Case 83: Using Perl-Compatible Regular Expressions (PCRE)
cases.what: Employs Perl regular expressions to catch structured digits like Social Security Numbers (\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}).
parts: -P : Activates Perl-Compatible Regular Expression (PCRE) engine capabilities.

cases.title: Use Case 84: Matching lines that begin with specific characters
cases.what: Matches lines that start exactly with the word bracket "[START]".
parts: ^ : Line-start anchor forcing patterns to match from the far-left position.
\[ : Escapes the special regex bracket token to search for a literal left bracket character.

cases.title: Use Case 85: Matching lines that end with specific strings
cases.what: Targets rows where the line ends exactly with the characters "failed".
parts: $ : Line-end anchor forcing patterns to match against the far-right edge of a line.

cases.title: Use Case 86: Matching lines containing pure numeric character fields
cases.what: Filters a file to show only lines composed entirely of numbers.
parts: ^[0-9]+$ : Matches a line that contains one or more digits from start to end without spaces or letters.

cases.title: Use Case 87: Executing multiple explicit search expressions
cases.what: Combines multiple distinct search queries to catch lines containing either "WARN" or "FAIL".
parts: -e : Protects and declares individual search expressions. Useful for strings starting with a hyphen.

cases.title: Use Case 88: Using lookahead assertions in Perl mode
cases.what: Matches the word "user" only if it is immediately followed by "=admin", without including "=admin" in the output.
parts: (?==admin) : Positive lookahead assertion that validates the trailing string context without consuming it.

cases.title: Use Case 89: Extracting bounded alphanumeric hash elements
cases.what: Finds and extracts 32-character hexadecimal strings (like MD5 hashes) from a log file.
parts: \b : Word boundary markers preventing matches on longer character structures.
[a-f0-9]{32} : Matches exactly 32 consecutive hexadecimal characters.

cases.title: Use Case 90: Matching empty or whitespace-only lines
cases.what: Finds lines that are completely blank or contain only tabs and spaces.
parts: ^[[:blank:]]*$: Evaluates a line from start to end to see if it contains zero or more blank spacing characters.

cases.title: Use Case 91: Silently validating text inside conditional bash statements
cases.command: if grep -q "SUCCESS" deployment.log; then echo "Verification passed."; fi
cases.what: Checks for a word in a file and runs a conditional branch without printing the matched text to the terminal.
parts: -q : Quiet mode flag. Exits immediately with a zero status code if a match is found, without printing output.

cases.title: Use Case 92: Extracting process IDs via system pipeline filters
cases.what: Finds the process ID of the mysql daemon safely, without catching the grep process itself in the results.
parts: [m]ysqld : Regex trick where the brackets prevent grep from matching its own command-line entry string.

cases.title: Use Case 93: Counting specific connection records from network streams
cases.what: Counts active network connections by checking for the word "ESTABLISHED" in netstat output.
parts: | : Standard shell pipeline redirecting netstat stdout into grep stdin.

cases.title: Use Case 94: Colorizing matches explicitly for programmatic view wrappers
cases.what: Forces grep to keep color highlights when piping output to an interactive pager like less.
parts: --color=always: Injects ANSI color escape sequences into the output stream.
less -R : Tells less to display the raw ANSI color sequences correctly instead of printing text escape codes.

cases.title: Use Case 95: Tracking live incoming stream additions via log trailing
cases.what: Monitors a log file in real time and immediately outputs any new rows that contain a "404" error.
parts: --line-buffered: Forces grep to flush its output buffer on every line, preventing lag when piping live data.

cases.what: Globally changes grep's default match highlight color to bright bold red.
parts: GREP_COLORS : Environment configuration variable managing color outputs ('ms=01;31' specifies bold red).

cases.title: Use Case 97: Counting non-blank lines in code trees
cases.what: Counts the total number of lines in a file that are not empty.
parts: -v : Selects lines that do not match the pattern.
-c : Counts those lines, effectively returning the non-empty line count.

cases.title: Use Case 98: Restricting processing paths using file descriptor redirection

parts: ([0-9]{1,3}.){3}: Matches a group of 1 to 3 numbers followed by a literal dot, repeated exactly 3 times.
