commands.name: lsof
commands.description: lsof lists open file descriptors. The name “file” includes sockets, pipes, and device handles, so process ownership can explain why a path or port is still busy.

anatomy.label: Names and filters
anatomy.text: A pathname, PID, user, or network selector narrows the open-descriptor list. “File” includes sockets, pipes, and devices.

anatomy.label: Network options
anatomy.text: `-i` selects network files, `-nP` avoids DNS/service-name lookups, and `-sTCP:LISTEN` filters TCP state.

anatomy.label: Permissions
anatomy.text: Process ownership and command details may be hidden unless the caller has enough privilege; start with ordinary access and elevate only when needed.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Victor A. Abell

origins.label: When
origins.text: Development is documented from 1994.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: To show which processes hold files open. On Unix-like systems, that includes ordinary files, devices, pipes, and network sockets.

cases.title: Use Case 01: List internet sockets
cases.what: List internet sockets.
parts: The `-i` selector reports Internet network files and sockets across IPv4 and IPv6.
It may include listeners and established connections; use a state filter to narrow it.

cases.title: Use Case 02: Identify a listener on one port
cases.what: Identify a listener on one port.
parts: `-iTCP:8080` selects TCP port 8080, `-sTCP:LISTEN` limits results to listeners, and `-nP` avoids host and service-name lookups.

cases.title: Use Case 03: List TCP network files
cases.what: List TCP network files.
parts: The protocol selector narrows network entries to TCP.
It does not limit results to listeners.

cases.title: Use Case 04: Find a connection to a remote host
cases.what: Find a connection to a remote host.
parts: The `@` selector matches the remote address; 192.0.2.50 is reserved for documentation, so replace it with an address you are authorized to inspect.

cases.title: Use Case 05: Show established TCP connections
cases.what: Show established TCP connections.
parts: The state filter omits listeners and other TCP states, leaving established connections visible.

cases.title: Use Case 06: Inspect a port range
cases.what: Inspect a port range.
parts: The port selector covers the inclusive range; numeric output makes the endpoints easier to compare.

cases.title: Use Case 07: Keep port numbers numeric
cases.what: Keep port numbers numeric.
parts: `-P` suppresses service-name conversion for ports.
Add `-n` as well when host-name resolution should also be skipped.

cases.title: Use Case 08: List open files for a user
cases.what: List open files for a user.
parts: The user selector matches processes owned by that account.
Substitute a real account name; visibility depends on permissions.

cases.title: Use Case 09: Inspect one process file table
cases.what: Inspect one process file table.
parts: `-p` selects a process ID.
Replace PID with one you have confirmed; results may include files, pipes, sockets, and devices.

cases.title: Use Case 10: Select processes by command name
cases.what: Select processes by command name.
parts: `-c` filters by process command name, which may differ from a graphical application’s displayed name.

cases.title: Use Case 11: Inspect several process IDs
cases.what: Inspect several process IDs.
parts: A comma-separated list selects those PIDs.
Replace the examples with verified process IDs from the same system.

cases.title: Use Case 12: Find users of a directory’s immediate entries
cases.what: Find users of a directory’s immediate entries.
parts: `+d` checks the directory and its immediate entries.
It does not descend through every subdirectory.

cases.title: Use Case 13: Search a small tree recursively
cases.what: Search a small tree recursively.
parts: `+D` walks the full tree and can be slow on large directories or network mounts; restrict it to a small target.

cases.title: Use Case 14: Find unlinked files still held open
cases.what: Find unlinked files still held open.
parts: The link-count selector finds open files whose names have been unlinked.
A process can keep their storage allocated until its final descriptor closes.

cases.title: Use Case 15: Skip host and service-name lookups
cases.what: Skip host and service-name lookups.
parts: `-n` keeps network addresses numeric and `-P` keeps port numbers numeric, which speeds inspection and avoids ambiguous name resolution.

cases.title: Use Case 16: Require both user and command selectors
cases.what: Require both user and command selectors.
parts: By default, lsof can combine selection sets with OR; `-a` requests AND behavior so the result must satisfy both selectors.

cases.title: Use Case 17: Return only PIDs for a listener
cases.what: Return only PIDs for a listener.
parts: `-t` emits process IDs only, suitable for a script to inspect further.
Review the IDs before signaling any process; do not pipe blindly into a force-kill command.

cases.title: Use Case 18: Exclude the root account
cases.what: Exclude the root account.
parts: The caret negates the user selector.
This can produce a large result set, so pair it with a path or network selector when possible.

cases.title: Use Case 19: Refresh a port view every five seconds
cases.what: Refresh a port view every five seconds.
parts: `-r 5` repeats the report at five-second intervals.
Stop the live command with Ctrl-C.

cases.title: Use Case 20: Select by numeric user ID
cases.what: Select by numeric user ID.
parts: A numeric UID can select an account without relying on its login name; confirm the UID mapping on the current host.

cases.title: Use Case 21: 18.6 Network & Open Ports
cases.what: 18.6 Network & Open Ports.
parts: List all listening ports.

cases.title: Use Case 22: 1. Deleted Execution Recovery
cases.what: 1. Deleted Execution Recovery.
parts: This pipeline sends output from `lsof` to `grep`; each stage receives the previous stage’s standard output as input.

cases.title: Use Case 23: Listing all open files on the system
cases.what: Displays a massive snapshot of every single open file, network socket, pipe, and system library currently held open by active processes.
parts: lsof : The base command utility invocation (List Open Files).

cases.title: Use Case 24: Finding which processes are using a specific file
cases.what: Identifies every active system process or thread currently reading from or writing to a targeted file.
parts: /var/log/... : The absolute or relative file path being queried for active locks.

cases.title: Use Case 25: Listing all files open under a specific directory tree
cases.what: Scans the top layer of a directory to see which files are actively being held open by running processes.
parts: +d : Directory flag restriction. It checks the specified directory folder but does not recurse down subdirectories.

cases.title: Use Case 26: Recursively listing open files across an entire directory tree
cases.what: Deep-scans a directory and all of its subfolders to find every open file descriptor across the entire directory structure.
parts: +D : Recursive directory flag modifier that forces full directory tree validation matching.

cases.title: Use Case 27: Filtering open files by a specific process name
cases.what: Isolates and tracks open files used exclusively by processes whose execution name begins with "nginx".
parts: -c : Command name filter selector flag.
nginx : The process command string descriptor to look up.

cases.title: Use Case 28: Listing open files for a specific process name using case-insensitive matches
cases.what: Finds open files for processes like "mysql", "MySQL", or "MYSQL" by ignoring text casing rules.
parts: -C : Disables case sensitivity configurations for the command (-c) name lookups.

cases.title: Use Case 29: Filtering open files by a precise Process ID (PID)
cases.what: Extracts the complete list of files, libraries, and sockets allocated to a specific process identifier.
parts: -p : Process ID selection filter flag.
2048 : The targeted numeric Process ID integer.

cases.title: Use Case 30: Inverting the Process ID search filter using negation
cases.what: Lists every open file descriptor on the entire system *except* those allocated to PID 1 (init/systemd).
parts: ^ : The negation operator used inside lsof option values to exclude specific entries.

cases.title: Use Case 31: Listing files held open by a specific system user
cases.what: Audits active system profiles by listing every file currently opened by the "webadmin" user account.
parts: -u : User selection profile lookup filter flag.
webadmin : The targeted system username.

cases.title: Use Case 32: Filtering connections by an explicit IP network version
cases.what: Restricts the network monitoring query to show only IPv4 socket connections.
parts: 4 : Restricts the internet selection flag (-i) to IPv4 protocols exclusively.

cases.title: Use Case 33: Restricting network socket audits to IPv6 connections
cases.what: Restricts the network monitoring query to show only IPv6 socket connections.
parts: 6 : Restricts the internet selection flag (-i) to IPv6 protocols exclusively.

cases.title: Use Case 34: Finding which process is listening on an exact network port
cases.what: Pinpoints the exact web server or process that is currently binding to and using network port 80.
parts: :80 : Specifies the exact network port number to inspect, preceded by a colon.

cases.title: Use Case 35: Auditing active TCP protocol socket streams exclusively
cases.what: Screens out UDP traffic to show only connection-oriented TCP socket allocations.
parts: TCP : Protocol type constraint applied directly to the internet selection parameter.

cases.title: Use Case 36: Auditing raw UDP protocol socket allocations
cases.what: Screens out TCP traffic to look for stateless UDP data channels or DNS lookups.
parts: UDP : Protocol type constraint targeting user datagram traffic structures.

cases.title: Use Case 37: Tracking a combination of precise network ports and protocols
cases.what: Pinpoints processes handling secure web traffic by filtering for TCP connections on port 443.
parts: TCP:443 : Combines protocol type constraints and target port indices inside a single statement.

cases.title: Use Case 38: Checking connection loops over a specific range of ports
cases.what: Audits privileged system ports by checking for active network connections between ports 1 and 1024.
parts: 1-1024 : Specifies a range of network ports to scan.

cases.title: Use Case 39: Suppressing network port and name resolution lookups for speed
cases.what: Speeds up port lookups dramatically by skipping slow DNS lookups and displaying raw numeric IP addresses and port numbers.
parts: -n : Inhibits the conversion of network numbers to hostnames (disables DNS reverse lookups).
-P : Inhibits the conversion of port numbers to service names (e.g., shows 22 instead of "ssh").

cases.title: Use Case 40: Finding active connections established with a specific remote host
cases.what: Identifies files and sockets linked to data streams flowing to or from a specific remote IP address.
parts: @192.168... : Specifies the targeted remote host IP address or hostname criteria.

cases.title: Use Case 41: Combining separate option rules using strict AND logic
cases.what: Finds only the active *network sockets* that belong specifically to the user *webadmin*.
parts: -a : Changes the global option matching logic from an OR match (default) to a strict conditional AND match.
-u / -i : Separate search parameters linked together by the boolean AND operator.

cases.title: Use Case 42: Listing open files by their explicit file type categorization
cases.what: Returns a clean list of PIDs for processes that are holding open regular plain text documents.
parts: -d txt : Filters file listings by exact structural file extensions or file descriptor text tags.

cases.title: Use Case 43: Listing open unix domain sockets locally
cases.what: Lists inter-process communication channels (Unix Domain Sockets) active on the local machine.
parts: -U : Selects the listing of UNIX domain socket file descriptors explicitly.

cases.title: Use Case 44: Extracting clean, raw list arrays of PIDs for automation scripting
cases.what: Outputs just the raw process ID numbers for nginx, making it easy to pipe directly into termination loops.
parts: -t : Terse output modifier. Suppresses table layout headers and columns to return raw PID integers only.

cases.title: Use Case 45: Grouping lookups across multiple explicit Process IDs
cases.what: Audits a specific cluster of processes simultaneously using a comma-separated list of PIDs.
parts: 512,1024... : Comma-separated list configuration allowing batched multi-ID validation passes.

cases.title: Use Case 46: Monitoring open files based on directory mount nodes
cases.what: Identifies every single process actively accessing the /home partition, which is useful when trying to unmount a busy drive.
parts: /home : Path reference pointing to a dedicated drive mount node layer.

cases.title: Use Case 47: Finding files opened by a specific Group ID (GID)
cases.what: Finds files opened by processes running under primary system Group ID 1001.
parts: -g : Group identification lookup selector.

cases.title: Use Case 48: Monitoring file locks applied by database engines
cases.what: Audits active file locks across the system to help troubleshoot database lockups or file sharing conflicts.
parts: -V : Verbose helper flag that reports hidden file locks or validation check statuses.

cases.title: Use Case 49: Checking files opened within a specific terminal screen interface
cases.what: Audits terminal activity by listing all files and utilities running inside virtual terminal session "pts/1".
parts: /dev/pts/1 : Direct pseudo-terminal device file location marker path.

cases.title: Use Case 50: Killing all processes locking a specific network port on-the-fly
cases.what: Immediately frees up a blocked port (like 8080) by finding and killing whatever process is sitting on it.
parts: -t -i :8080 : Collects raw process IDs attached to port 8080.
xargs kill -9: Passes those PIDs directly into a forceful kill execution loop.

cases.title: Use Case 51: Safely checking if a configuration folder is busy before running updates
cases.command: if lsof +d /etc/nginx > /dev/null; then echo "Configuration files are currently busy."; fi
cases.what: Performs a safe check to ensure configuration files aren't being modified before starting automated service runs.
parts: /dev/null : Discards standard output to use lsof purely for its conditional exit status code.

cases.title: Use Case 52: Calculating the total count of open sockets across the entire machine
cases.what: Counts the total number of open network connections currently active on the machine.
parts: wc -l : Counts the incoming rows to return a single total integer count.

cases.title: Use Case 53: Safely unmounting a busy drive by killing active file lockers
cases.what: Sends a polite termination signal (SIGTERM) to all processes accessing a backup drive so it can be unmounted safely.
parts: kill -15 : Sends a standard termination signal to allow applications to save data and close gracefully.

cases.title: Use Case 54: Tracking memory leaks by counting file descriptors per process name
cases.what: Helps find file descriptor leaks in applications by counting how many resource targets they are holding open.
parts: -c java : Tracks open descriptors allocated to Java execution workers.

cases.title: Use Case 55: Formatting open connection listings directly into clean JSON arrays
cases.what: Converts raw connection tables into clean JSON objects that are easy to parse with API backends.
parts: awk 'NR>1...' : Skips table headers and uses print layout configurations to wrap the columns in JSON syntax.

cases.title: Use Case 56: Monitoring live file access interactions in real time
cases.what: Monitors an authentication log continuously, refreshing every 2 seconds to show active reading or writing processes.
parts: -r 2 : Repeat option modifier flag. It loops and re-runs the lsof query continuously at 2-second intervals.

cases.title: Use Case 57: Stopping the repeat loop instantly once a match is discovered
cases.what: Monitors a temporary directory continuously until a specific file name or pattern is accessed.
parts: -r 1 : Refreshes the directory scan every 1 second.

cases.title: Use Case 58: Counting how many distinct files a single process ID is using
cases.what: Checks the resource usage of your current active shell instance ($$) by counting its open file descriptors.
parts: $$ : Standard shell variable representing the PID of your current shell session.

cases.title: Use Case 59: Generating automated alert updates whenever unlinked space hogs grow too large
cases.command: lsof +L1 | awk '$7 > 104857600 {print "PID " $2 " holds a deleted file of size " $7 " bytes"}'
cases.what: Identifies hidden processes holding onto deleted files that are larger than 100MB and taking up disk space.
parts: $7 > ... : Evaluates the size column (7th column) against a 100 Megabyte byte threshold.

cases.title: Use Case 60: Recovering accidentally deleted text contents out of active proc nodes
cases.what: Recovers a deleted file by copying it out of the Linux proc filesystem, using the PID and file descriptor discovered by lsof.
parts: /proc/... : The kernel virtual storage pathway where lsof identifies the process file descriptor link location.

cases.title: Use Case 61: Auditing shared library tracks mapping into active memory layers
cases.what: Lists all shared libraries (.so files) currently mapped into process memory spaces across the system.
parts: -d mem : Restricts lookups to memory-mapped files and shared execution objects.

cases.title: Use Case 62: Auditing connections linked to specific service names natively
cases.what: Finds active connections by using standard service names (like ssh) instead of numeric port numbers.
parts: :ssh : Maps service name strings directly to port indices using the system services database (/etc/services).

cases.title: Use Case 63: Isolating active raw network packets listening sockets
cases.what: Identifies processes opening raw network sockets, which is useful for catching unauthorized packet sniffers or tools like Wireshark.
parts: -d raw : Tracks raw network protocol communication descriptors.

cases.title: Use Case 64: Finding files opened with read-only access permissions
cases.what: Filters the standard file descriptor table to show only files opened with strict read-only access rules.
parts: "r " : Matches the read-only execution state indicator inside the table access mode column field.

cases.title: Use Case 65: Tracking files opened with active write access privileges
cases.what: Filters the file descriptor table to find files opened with write permissions, indicating active updates or modifications.
parts: "w" : Matches the write access mode flag symbol in lsof output tables.

cases.title: Use Case 66: Pinpointing the execution paths of active binary files on disk
cases.what: Verifies exactly which executable binaries are running out of the primary system bin directory.
parts: /usr/bin : Filters for binary executables mapped into the memory layout layer.

cases.title: Use Case 67: Listing all files open on character devices
cases.what: Identifies processes talking directly to hardware character devices, such as serial ports or terminal nodes.
parts: -d chr : Restricts file listings to character device drivers.

cases.title: Use Case 68: Checking network sockets locked in an established state
cases.what: Filters network connections to show only active, established communication sessions, ignoring idle listeners.
parts: "ESTABLISHED": Text string signature identifying active connection states inside the network status column.

commands.name: nmap
commands.description: nmap sends network probes to discover hosts, open ports, and services. Use only against systems and address ranges you are authorized to assess; scans can trigger alerts or affect fragile devices. Confirm scope and choose a bounded scan before sending traffic.

anatomy.label: [SCAN OPTIONS]
anatomy.text: Selects discovery, port scanning, service/version detection, scripts, timing, or output. Options change the traffic sent and the evidence collected; begin with a narrow, authorized scope.

anatomy.label: [TARGET SPECIFICATION…]
anatomy.text: One or more explicitly authorized hostnames, addresses, ranges, or CIDR networks. A target file can be supplied with `-iL`; review its contents before starting a scan.

anatomy.label: Results and privilege
anatomy.text: Nmap reports observations such as `open`, `closed`, or `filtered`; these are network observations, not proof that a service is safe or vulnerable. Some scan methods need elevated privileges. Scans can trigger alerts or affect fragile systems.

anatomy.label: Output
anatomy.text: Use `-oN` for readable text, `-oX` for XML, or `-oA` for several formats. Grepable `-oG` output is retained for compatibility but is deprecated.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: First published in Phrack magazine Issue 51; the project history does not establish the city where Lyon wrote it.

origins.label: Why it emerged

commands.name: nslookup
commands.description: nslookup queries DNS using the configured resolver or an explicitly selected server. Record type and resolver selection change the question and answer.

anatomy.label: [OPTION…]
anatomy.text: Options select output, filtering, or operation details; check this implementation’s help because flags vary by program.

anatomy.label: [ARGUMENT…]
anatomy.text: Operands supply the paths, names, records, or values the command acts on. Confirm the target and the expected output before a state-changing invocation.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: No single author for the command is credited in the BIND history cited here; it belongs to the collaborative BIND DNS software lineage.

origins.label: When
origins.text: BIND began as a UC Berkeley project in the early 1980s; an exact first `nslookup` release date is not established here.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: University of California, Berkeley, initially under a DARPA grant.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: To let an operator query DNS nameservers interactively or from a command line while diagnosing name-to-address and related record lookups.

cases.what: Query a DNS name.
parts: The answer depends on the resolver configured for this host.

cases.what: Query mail exchanger records.

cases.what: Query an IPv6 address record.

parts: example.com : The target domain lookup target.
8.8.8.8 : The explicit IP address of the target DNS server being used for the query.

parts: -type=aaaa : Limits the lookup target query schema to quad-A (IPv6) address mappings.

cases.what: Identifies the mail servers responsible for handling inbound email delivery for a domain.
parts: -type=mx : Restricts the lookup profile to track down Mail Exchanger (MX) configuration layouts.

cases.what: Resolves a numeric IP address back to its associated domain name structure.
parts: 93.184.216.34: The target IPv4 address passed directly as the lookup argument parameter.

cases.command: if nslookup example.com > /dev/null; then echo "Domain resolves correctly."; fi
cases.what: Tests whether a domain can be resolved to determine if the network or a targeted website is available.
parts: /dev/null : Hides screen output to use the command purely for its true/false exit status code.

parts: $(...) : Command substitution wrapper capturing standard output streams into bash contexts.
+short : Ensures that only the raw numbers are returned without trailing notes or labels.

parts: != : Unary comparison operator that checks if two strings are unequal.

parts: watch -n 5 : Automatically re-executes the targeted command string every 5 seconds.

commands.description: ollama controls a local model service. list and show inspect available models; run can load a model and consume substantial memory or start an interactive session.

origins.label: Creator(s)

origins.label: When

origins.label: Where

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: To make supported open models straightforward to run locally and usable by applications through a local API.

cases.title: Use Case 05: Downloading an LLM model from the central registry
cases.what: Downloads the specific model weights and manifest sheets into your local machine's storage bank.
parts: ollama : The base command utility invocation interface.

llama3 : The model tag name identifier being fetched.

cases.title: Use Case 06: Starting an interactive terminal chat session
cases.what: Loads the model into your active system memory (RAM/VRAM) and spawns an interactive REPL chat session.
parts: run : Combined command that pulls (if missing), mounts, and executes a conversation loop.

cases.title: Use Case 07: Removing a model from local storage to free up space
cases.what: Purges the selected model weights and structural layers out of your system partition.
parts: rm : The removal command directive.
gemma : The model identifier tag targeted for destruction.

cases.title: Use Case 08: Copying an existing model to a new custom tag descriptor
cases.what: Generates a structural reference pointer duplicating a model descriptor mapping without cloning the raw weight layers.
parts: cp : Replication command option.

cases.title: Use Case 09: Passing a single text prompt to an execution loop directly from stdout
cases.command: ollama run llama3 "Write a 3-word slogan for Linux"
cases.what: Executes a single generation pass non-interactively and sends the string output directly back to the terminal.
parts: "Write..." : Trailing prompt string argument that bypasses interactive shell setups.

cases.title: Use Case 10: Verifying details and configuration parameters of a specific local model
cases.what: Exposes model manifest configuration blocks, including architecture types, quantization tiers, license templates, and parameters.
parts: show : Diagnostic metadata presentation sub-command.

cases.title: Use Case 11: Spawning the background server daemon manually
cases.what: Initializes the underlying orchestration engine network worker and binds it to its native local communication ports.
parts: serve : Engine service hosting routine initialization.

cases.title: Use Case 12: Creating a custom model variation from a local configuration script
cases.what: Parses a local configuration script (`Modelfile`) to compile a brand-new, customized LLM entry point.
parts: create : Model structural build system command.
custom-bot : The unique custom identifier tag name assigned to the output model.
-f ./Modelfile: Path argument pointing directly to your instruction manifest block.

cases.title: Use Case 13: Defining a foundational system prompt inside a Modelfile configuration
cases.command: # SYSTEM You are a strict Linux SysAdmin assistant. Only output bash commands.
cases.what: Injects a permanent, un-erasable system context constraint rule layer directly into a custom model build.
parts: SYSTEM : Modelfile keyword instruction configuring the base assistant persona mask.

cases.title: Use Case 14: Hardcoding temperature settings inside a Modelfile parameters block
cases.what: Adjusts model generation parameters to lower creativity and enforce highly deterministic, accurate responses.
parts: PARAMETER : Modelfile parameter declaration keyword prefix.
temperature : The exact generation variable configuration target.

cases.title: Use Case 15: Adjusting context length windows explicitly via parameter files
cases.what: Expands a model's operational context limit threshold up to 8,192 tokens to support processing longer document payloads.
parts: num_ctx : Model structural configuration key defining token window boundary weights.

cases.title: Use Case 16: Injecting a custom stopping token match criteria into configurations
cases.what: Adds a structural sequence listener that forces the model to stop generating text as soon as the specified token is hit.
parts: stop : Token evaluation parameter mapping termination conditions.

cases.title: Use Case 17: Pulling a baseline model dynamically inside a Modelfile template
cases.what: Defines the base foundational model template layer that your custom parameters and system prompts will build on top of.
parts: FROM : Crucial Modelfile initialization keyword pointing to source weights configurations.

cases.title: Use Case 18: Configuring token generation limits inside instruction sheets
cases.what: Protects computing resources by capping the maximum number of tokens a model can output in a single completion pass.
parts: num_predict : Output allocation threshold variable.

cases.title: Use Case 19: Setting custom prompt formatting layouts inside Modelfiles
cases.what: Hardcodes explicit instruction wrappers to match the token syntax requirements of specific model architectures.
parts: TEMPLATE : Structural prompt engineering syntax controller directive.

cases.title: Use Case 20: Building model variations using external base GGUF partition layers
cases.what: Imports external quantized model data sheets compiled outside Ollama directly into your native local runtime engines.
parts: ./arbi... : Relative path target to an independent, pre-quantized GGUF binary file.

cases.title: Use Case 21: Overriding system licenses descriptions within custom model packages
cases.what: Documents license parameters inside the compiled model metadata manifest tables.
parts: LICENSE : Regulatory specification metadata assignment token.

cases.title: Use Case 22: Querying raw text generation via local cURL network requests
cases.what: Sends a text prompt to the background service API endpoint and streams the token response blocks back to stdout.
parts: http://localhost:11434: The default network communication socket address bound by the daemon process.
/api/generate: Native single-prompt compilation endpoint endpoint destination.
-d '...' : JSON data payload containing the target model and instructions.

cases.title: Use Case 23: Requesting formal chat structures with roles distributions via APIs
cases.what: Executes structured conversations by passing explicit role mappings (system, user, assistant) to the model.
parts: /api/chat : Stateful chat endpoint node supporting comprehensive conversation logs arrays.

cases.title: Use Case 24: Disabling token streaming responses inside API connection payloads
cases.what: Forces the API to wait until the entire response is generated before returning a single, consolidated JSON block.
parts: "stream": false: Boolean parameter configuration turning off incremental connection emissions.

cases.title: Use Case 25: Generating vector mathematical embeddings from text targets via APIs
cases.what: Passes text data to an embedding model to extract its mathematical vector coordinate mapping array for RAG workloads.
parts: /api/embeddings: Specialized endpoint used to transform text tokens into numerical float arrays.

cases.title: Use Case 26: Checking local server status configurations via minimal endpoint polls
cases.what: Performs a fast network lookup against the server to programmatically retrieve your local model list in JSON format.
parts: /api/tags : System catalog configuration map endpoint destination.

cases.title: Use Case 27: Feeding local text file payloads directly into an LLM via pipelines
cases.command: cat server_logs.txt | ollama run llama3 "Summarize these logs for errors"
cases.what: Pipes raw text contents into an evaluation pass to summarize logs or extract data automatically.
parts: cat ... : Dumps target documentation text data into standard outputs streams.
| : Redirects stdout data directly into the stdin buffer of your Ollama container.

cases.title: Use Case 28: Automated code auditing scripts generation via output redirections
cases.command: ollama run MODEL "Review this code and suggest a patch:" < ./lab/script.sh > ./lab/audited_script.suggested.sh
cases.what: Uses command substitution to pull code into a prompt, gets fixes from the model, and writes the output directly back to a script file.
parts: $(cat ...) : Bash inline execution pattern nesting text streams directly inside string arguments.

cases.title: Use Case 29: Silently validating formatting patterns inside conditional bash structures
cases.command: if ollama run llama3 "Is '$(date)' a weekend? Answer yes or no" | grep -q -i "yes"; then echo "Cron skips."; fi
cases.what: Routes background automation behaviors by letting a local model evaluate dynamic script arguments on the fly.
parts: grep -q : Quiet mode text selection flag that turns string checks into conditional true/false exit codes.

cases.title: Use Case 30: Monitoring model processing execution latency ticks using time blocks
cases.what: Benchmarks performance by measuring the exact system execution time and processor ticks spent running a query.
parts: time : Built-in bash resource utilization reporting utility.

cases.title: Use Case 31: Iterating through bulk document stacks inside automated file loops
cases.command: for f in ./tickets/*.txt; do [ -f "$f" ] || continue; ollama run MODEL "Triage this ticket:" < "$f" > "$f.reply"; done
cases.what: Loops through a directory of support tickets, processes each file with an LLM, and saves the generated response alongside it.
parts: for f in... : Standard shell iteration loop used to batch-process files.

cases.title: Use Case 32: Running multimodal image analysis models directly from terminal contexts
cases.what: Passes a local image file path to a vision-language model (VLM) to analyze its visual contents.
parts: llava : Multimodal vision-capable model library tag identifier.
@ : Prefix operator token telling the engine that the following text string points to a local file path.

cases.title: Use Case 33: Laundering environment host configurations to support broad network access
cases.what: Binds the Ollama API to all interfaces. The local API does not provide general-purpose authentication by default; restrict access with network controls and do not expose it directly to the Internet.
parts: OLLAMA_HOST : Internal environment control variable managing network socket configuration targets.
0.0.0.0 : Binding wildcard directive opening availability across all network interfaces.

cases.title: Use Case 34: Routing computational paths across explicit dedicated graphic nodes
cases.what: Sets a CUDA device visibility variable before starting Ollama. This is backend and platform dependent; verify the selected GPU with runtime logs and `ollama ps`.
parts: CUDA_VIS... : Low-level driver environment control selector flag.

cases.title: Use Case 35: Pre-loading models into system memory permanently to bypass initialization lag
cases.what: Instructs the engine to keep a model loaded in memory indefinitely, eliminating the usual startup delay for future requests.
parts: "keep_alive": -1: Special duration integer value that disables automatic memory eviction timers.

cases.title: Use Case 36: Evicting all active models from system memory instantly
cases.what: Instantly frees up your system's RAM/VRAM by forcing the engine to unload the specified model immediately.
parts: "keep_alive": 0: Setting the duration parameter to zero triggers an immediate model eviction command.

cases.title: Use Case 37: Extracting clean, non-interactive markdown logs inside project workspaces
cases.what: Instructs the model's generation parameters to guarantee that the output matches a clean, valid structural JSON format layout.
parts: --format json: Strict syntax constraint modifier enforced over generation arrays.

cases.title: Use Case 38: Evaluating model allocation metrics inside orchestrators
cases.what: Starts the service engine daemon in high-verbosity debug mode to stream internal kernel scheduling logs directly to stderr.
parts: OLLAMA_DEBUG : Environment configuration value activating low-level trace logging.

cases.title: Use Case 39: Managing text generation using Python scripting wrappers
cases.what: Runs a rapid text generation check using Ollama's official Python library wrapper directly inside a terminal line.
parts: python -c : Executes inline Python code blocks without creating a physical script file on disk.

cases.title: Use Case 40: Generating photorealistic imagery directly inside terminal displays
cases.command: ollama run z-image-turbo "A futuristic city in autumn, film style"
cases.what: Uses a model that supports image generation only when the installed Ollama version and model provide that capability. Generated files are not necessarily displayed in a text terminal.
parts: z-image-turbo: Advanced text-to-image weight library model definition block.

cases.title: Use Case 41: Laundering environment variables to handle alternative model folder paths
cases.what: Redirects the model storage path to an external drive to preserve space on your main boot drive partition.
parts: OLLAMA_MODELS: Internal path variable configuration tracking where model layers are saved on disk.

cases.title: Use Case 42: Downloading an AI model from the library registry without running it
cases.what: Downloads the specific model layers from the official repository library directly to your local drive without opening an interactive session.
parts: ollama pull : Inbound registry image fetch download utility.
llama3.3:8b : Targeted model namespace indicator string and parameter scale tag assignment.

cases.title: Use Case 43: Downloading a model using shorthand defaults
cases.what: Pulls a model while letting Ollama automatically select the safest, most stable default quantization layer (typically the 4-bit GGUF build).
parts: gemma2 : Slices the target model registry directory using its default canonical layout tag.

cases.title: Use Case 44: Launching an interactive chat terminal session (Automatic download fallback)
cases.what: Initializes a model inside memory and boots up a live interactive chat environment directly in your shell prompt; automatically downloads the model first if missing.
parts: ollama run : Core execution engine engine initialization directive.
llama3.2 : The targeted local or remote open-weight model name tag selection.

cases.title: Use Case 45: Deleting a model to free up local disk sectors
cases.what: Purges all matching weight layers from your storage paths, immediately returning hard drive sectors.
parts: ollama rm : Remove model layer destruction command macro.
cases.note: Removes local model files for the selected tag. Confirm the model name before running.

cases.title: Use Case 46: Reviewing detailed structural manifest sheets for a model
cases.what: Details low-level architecture data including system prompt defaults, tokenizer configurations, context window size floors, and parameters weights mapping schemas.
parts: ollama show : Structural asset inspection query utility selector.

cases.title: Use Case 47: Extracting only the license profile data layer of a model
cases.what: Filters the show manifest data payload to display user rights assertions and compliance constraints directly.
parts: --license : Specific visibility filter modifier argument.

cases.title: Use Case 48: Extracting the raw default system prompt configurations
cases.what: Exposes the hidden internal base behavioral instructions managing the model's logic baseline.
parts: --system : Specific system prompt visibility query filter modifier.

cases.title: Use Case 49: Copying or renaming local models inside registries
cases.what: Generates a new pointer reference tag for an existing model footprint, allowing you to name custom variants without duplicating file sizes.
parts: ollama cp : Reference pointer duplicate/copy command tool.

cases.title: Use Case 50: Dispatching a single one-off prompt request from terminal parameters
cases.command: ollama run llama3.2 "Explain quantum computing in one sentence"
cases.what: Processes a prompt from a command argument instantly, prints the answer to stdout, and shuts down memory allocations immediately after completion.
parts: "Explain..." : String query literal directly intercepted by the model inference loop.

cases.title: Use Case 51: Piping text streams directly into models via standard input redirections
cases.command: echo "Analyze this code: console.log('hello')" | ollama run qwen2.5-coder
cases.what: Feeds data from an external shell utility straight into an inference engine, making it ideal for automation scripts.
parts: | : Standard Unix pipeline forwarding text stdout matrices into stdin ports.

cases.title: Use Case 52: Extracting code files into prompts directly using redirection operators
cases.what: Reads a text script directly from a file to process its content as a raw prompt string.
parts: < : Input redirection piping file buffers straight into the shell worker pipeline.

cases.title: Use Case 53: Initializing interactive prompts while forcing markdown layout output formatting
cases.command: ollama run llama3.2 --format json "Output a JSON list of 3 colors"
cases.what: Forces the underlying engine to use strict schema validation layers to guarantee that outputs conform to JSON formatting constraints.
parts: --format json: Restricts token generation logic structures to match structural JSON parameters.

cases.title: Use Case 54: Creating a custom AI persona script (The Modelfile Blueprint)
cases.command: cat << 'EOF' > Modelfile FROM llama3.2 PARAMETER temperature 0.2 PARAMETER num_ctx 8192 SYSTEM You are a strict code review assistant who only responds in YAML blocks. EOF
cases.what: Generates a custom configuration blueprint script (similar to a Dockerfile) defining base weights, altered temperature parameters, and unique target system behavior contexts.
parts: FROM : Model inheritance selector linking to active base layers.
PARAMETER : Sets internal inference variable weights like context size flags (`num_ctx`) or creativity weights (`temperature`).
SYSTEM : Defines the global base instruction set injected ahead of active chat sessions.

cases.title: Use Case 55: Compiling your custom Modelfile blueprint into a new model image
cases.what: Parses a Modelfile template configuration and saves a new, executable custom AI image under a custom name.
parts: ollama create: Image layer compiler system tool utility invocation.
code-reviewer: The custom name tag given to the newly generated model image.
-f : Path configuration switch pointing to the source file layout template. [1]

cases.title: Use Case 56: Adjusting internal context buffer ceilings via parameters updates
cases.what: Expands the model's active working memory layout to track much larger text structures concurrently.
parts: num_ctx : Number of tokens tracked across conversational histories.

cases.title: Use Case 57: Setting up stop token limits to control model generations
cases.what: Forces the model to stop generating tokens instantly whenever it outputs the specified text sequence.
parts: PARAMETER stop: Structural constraint preventing rogue loop runs during token generation cycles.

cases.title: Use Case 58: Adjusting penalization variables to reduce repetitive phrases
cases.what: Applies mathematical penalties to tokens that have already been used, forcing the engine to select more diverse vocabulary.
parts: repeat_penalty: High-precision control float managing vocabulary variation rates.

cases.title: Use Case 59: Verifying API service lifecycle availability via curl requests
cases.what: Pings the background Ollama network daemon to check if it is active and running correctly.
parts: 11434 : The standard default TCP networking port index allocated to local Ollama API instances. [2, 3, 4]

cases.title: Use Case 60: Dispatched a streaming text request to the generation API endpoint
cases.command: curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{ "model": "llama3.2", "prompt": "Why is the sky blue?" }'
cases.what: Sends a prompt to the generate API endpoint, which streams back token chunks in real time.
parts: /api/generate: Route managing raw generation inputs.
-d : Injects a data payload string containing standard JSON parameters. [5, 6]

cases.title: Use Case 61: Disabling data streaming to get a single complete JSON response
cases.what: Blocks incremental token chunks, forcing the API to wait and return a single unified JSON object once the full answer is complete.
parts: "stream": false: Boolean configuration flag disabling real-time network stream flushes.

cases.title: Use Case 62: Initiating formal multi-turn chat completions via API structures
cases.what: Sends a multi-turn chat history to the chat endpoint to get a response that maintains context awareness.
parts: /api/chat : Route managing conversational histories arrays mapping.
"messages" : Positional structural tracking rows capturing conversational history. [7]

cases.title: Use Case 63: Generating raw vector embeddings from text data fields
cases.what: Converts a text string into a high-dimensional vector array, which is useful for setting up retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) databases.
parts: /api/embeddings: Specialized vector feature endpoint path. [8]

cases.title: Use Case 64: Downloading registry images remotely via API service triggers
cases.what: Remotely triggers an automated background download loop for a model via standard network API queries.
parts: /api/pull : Programmatic endpoint interface managing image downloading channels.

cases.title: Use Case 65: Generating custom model definitions programmatically via API calls
cases.command: curl http://localhost:11434/api/create -d '{ "name": "api-bot", "modelfile": "FROM llama3.2\nSYSTEM You are an API assistant." }'
cases.what: Injects Modelfile string configurations directly over a network socket to build a new model image remotely.
parts: /api/create : Dynamic remote compilation endpoint path.

cases.title: Use Case 66: Deleting local assets remotely via API destruction triggers
cases.what: Sends a deletion directive over network sockets to remove a model image and clear up disk space.
parts: -X DELETE : Forces HTTP DELETE methods validation rules.

cases.title: Use Case 67: Retrieving diagnostic runtime status reports for a model via the API
cases.what: Fetches low-level architectural details and parameter configurations for an image via a clean JSON API payload.
parts: /api/show : Programmatic data mapping lookup route.

cases.title: Use Case 68: Silently validating tool availability inside shell scripts
cases.command: curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags >/dev/null && printf "Ollama API is responding\n"
cases.what: Checks the system's background processes to verify if the Ollama server daemon is active before running automation scripts.
parts: pgrep -x : Checks system process lists for exact string name matches.

cases.title: Use Case 69: Extracting raw generation strings dynamically inside local bash variables
cases.command: RESPONSE=$(ollama run llama3.2 "Get the current year out of 2026-10-10" | tr -d '\r')
cases.what: Captures a model's text response directly into a shell variable for downstream scripting tasks, stripping away extra carriage returns.
parts: tr -d '\r' : Pruning tool cleaning out hidden Dos carriage return spacing noise. [8]

cases.title: Use Case 70: Auto-downloading models conditionally if missing from local inventories
cases.command: ollama list | grep -q "deepseek-r1:8b" || ollama pull deepseek-r1:8b
cases.what: Scans your local inventory for a specific model and automatically starts downloading it only if it isn't found.
parts: grep -q : Silent matching flag that returns a true/false status code directly to the shell script conditional block.

cases.title: Use Case 71: Monitoring system resource offloading telemetry allocations
cases.what: Monitors hardware resource allocation (like VRAM on a GPU or active CPU threads) while Ollama is generating text.
parts: watch -n 1 : Automatically re-executes the targeted monitoring utility every 1 second. [9]

cases.title: Use Case 72: Aggregating multi-file analysis metrics inside rapid script loops
cases.command: for f in ./*.log; do [ -f "$f" ] || continue; printf "=== %s ===\n" "$f"; ollama run MODEL "Summarize errors in this log:" < "$f"; done
cases.what: Iterates through all log files in a directory, feeding each one into a model to automatically generate separate error summaries.
parts: < "$f" : Feeds the file data stream directly into the prompt engine input channel.

cases.title: Use Case 73: Formatting text inputs into structured JSON array strings programmatically
cases.command: curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/generate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model":"MODEL","prompt":"Return a JSON object with sample user fields","format":"json","stream":false}' | jq -r .response
cases.what: Requests a JSON response from a model and pipes it directly into jq for syntax validation and pretty printing.
parts: jq . : External JSON parser formatting output fields dynamically.

cases.title: Use Case 74: Verifying connection latencies across network interface loops
cases.what: Measures connection speed and generation latency to profile how fast the engine responds to a basic prompt.
parts: time : System metric monitoring tool capturing exact operational duration.

cases.title: Use Case 75: Programmatically cleaning out all installed models to clear disk space
cases.what: List model names for review before removing models. This read-only form avoids piping every installed model into a deletion command.
parts: awk 'NR>1' : Skips the table header line to isolate the raw model names.
xargs -I {} : Passes the model names one-by-one into the deletion command.
cases.note: The source version would remove every listed model. The included command is read-only; do not turn it into a bulk delete without reviewing each model.

cases.title: Use Case 76: Tailing internal system logs for troubleshooting background operations
cases.what: Monitors Ollama's background server logs in real time to debug issues like GPU driver errors or connection failures.
parts: ~/.ollama... : Standard storage path configuration route where background logs are kept on macOS.

cases.title: Use Case 77: Pre-loading models into memory to reduce initial prompt delays
cases.what: Pre-loads a model into your GPU or system memory and sets a 4-hour timeout, avoiding initial loading delays during automated workflows.
parts: "keep_alive" : Time configuration constraint variable keeping models open in memory. [9]

cases.title: Use Case 78: Passing images via API payloads using base64 encoding strings
cases.what: The API accepts base64 image data for compatible vision models. Put a real encoded image in the request file; the shortened sample string in the source is only a placeholder.
parts: "images" : Array parameter field containing base64 data strings.

cases.title: Use Case 79: Routing traffic to an Ollama server running on a custom network address
cases.what: Enforces an alternative destination network route, pointing the local CLI tool to a remote Ollama server instance on the network.
parts: OLLAMA_HOST : Environment configuration variable managing server connection routes.

cases.title: Use Case 80: Exposing your local Ollama server to your entire local network
cases.what: Configures Ollama to listen on all interfaces. This exposes the service to reachable networks; use a firewall and trusted network, and do not expose it directly to the Internet.
parts: 0.0.0.0 : Network binding shortcut pattern matching all active network connections.
cases.note: This changes the service’s network exposure. Restrict reachability with a firewall and trusted network; never expose the unauthenticated local API to the public Internet.

cases.title: Use Case 81: Offloading memory parsing workflows across multi-GPU setups
cases.what: Configures the engine to process up to 4 parallel request stream requests concurrently across your hardware threads.
parts: NUM_PARALLEL: Performance adjustment flag managing internal slot scheduling allocations.

cases.title: Use Case 82: Changing the folder path where downloaded model weights are saved
cases.what: Redirects the default download storage path to an external hard drive to protect your primary internal drive space.
parts: OLLAMA_MODELS: System path configuration override variable managing download targets.

cases.title: Use Case 83: Utilizing the optional paid cloud tier for datacenter models
cases.command: ollama run MODEL --cloud "Summarize this public sample text"
cases.what: Runs a model through Ollama cloud mode when that model and account support it. Prompts and related inputs are sent to the remote service; check current service terms and data handling before using sensitive text.
parts: --cloud : Preview modifier switch directing execution data matrices into hosted cloud engines. [3, 8, 11, 12]

cases.title: Use Case 84: Turning on "thinking toggle" loops for deep reasoning models
cases.command: curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/generate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model":"MODEL","prompt":"Explain the result briefly","think":true,"stream":false}' | jq -r .thinking,.response
cases.what: Requests the model’s supported thinking output through the generate API. Availability and representation depend on the model; returned reasoning text may be hidden or unavailable for some models.
parts: --thinking : Toggles visibility formatting controls for internal reasoning tokens. [8, 10]

commands.name: ps
commands.description: ps takes a snapshot of process metadata; it does not continuously monitor. Select processes and output fields deliberately, then use logs or tracing to explain behavior.

anatomy.label: Selection
anatomy.text: Options choose which processes to report; `-p PID` narrows to a known process.

anatomy.label: Output fields
anatomy.text: `-o` selects columns such as PID, parent, user, state, elapsed time, and command. ps is a snapshot, not a live monitor.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: For Linux procps, the manual credits Branko Lankester as the original author; later contributors substantially rewrote and extended it. The earlier Unix command has a separate lineage.

origins.label: When

origins.label: Where
origins.text: Linux procps project; the cited manual does not establish a specific development city.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: To take a snapshot of selected processes and their state. This answers a different question from a continuously refreshing monitor such as `top`.

commands.name: rsync
commands.description: rsync compares source and destination trees and transfers differences. A trailing slash changes whether the directory itself or its contents are copied; -n previews actions without applying them.

anatomy.label: SOURCE…` and `DESTINATION
anatomy.text: The trailing slash on a source directory changes whether its contents or the directory itself is placed at the destination.

anatomy.label: Options
anatomy.text: `-a` preserves common metadata, `-v` reports work, `-n` previews, and `--delete` removes destination-only paths.

anatomy.label: Agent practice
anatomy.text: Run the same command with `-n` first, inspect its output, then remove dry-run only after the source, destination, and deletion plan are correct.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Andrew Tridgell designed rsync and co-authored its original technical report with Paul Mackerras.

origins.label: When
origins.text: The rsync algorithm and report were published in June 1996.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: Department of Computer Science, Australian National University, Canberra, Australia.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: The algorithm transfers only the data needed to reconstruct changed files at the destination, enabling efficient synchronization over links with limited bandwidth.

commands.name: scp
commands.description: scp copies files over SSH. Confirm both endpoints and the remote account because a mistaken destination can overwrite data on another machine.

anatomy.label: Endpoint syntax
anatomy.text: A local path is written as a path; a remote path uses `[USER@]HOST:PATH`.

anatomy.label: Direction
anatomy.text: The source comes before the destination. Check both sides and the remote identity before a transfer that can overwrite data.

anatomy.label: Automation
anatomy.text: `-o BatchMode=yes` prevents an unattended run from waiting for an interactive password prompt.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: The original scp client is part of the SSH software family created by Tatu Ylönen; OpenSSH's implementation is maintained by the OpenBSD project.

origins.label: When
origins.text: Introduced with the early SSH toolset in the mid-1990s; OpenSSH's free implementation dates from 1999. The cited source does not establish a separate first-release year for scp.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: The SSH project began in Finland; OpenSSH is developed by the OpenBSD community in Canada.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: It copies files between systems through an SSH-protected connection. Modern OpenSSH scp uses SFTP by default, while retaining compatibility behavior when requested.

commands.name: sed
commands.description: sed reads a stream one line at a time, applies addressed commands to pattern space, then prints by default. -n disables that automatic print; s/old/new/ changes only the first match per line unless the g flag is added.

anatomy.label: SCRIPT
anatomy.text: An editing program applied to each input line. In `s/old/new/g`, `s` selects substitution, the delimiters separate the search and replacement, and `g` replaces every match on that line.

anatomy.label: [FILE…]
anatomy.text: Input files; with none, sed reads standard input. Without `-i`, edits are written to standard output and the original remains unchanged.

anatomy.label: Options
anatomy.text: `-n` suppresses automatic printing, so pair it with an explicit `p` command when selecting lines. In-place syntax differs between GNU and BSD sed.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Lee E. McMahon wrote the original implementation.

origins.label: When
origins.text: McMahon's Bell Labs memorandum documenting the design is dated August 15, 1978; reliable sources commonly place the implementation earlier in the 1970s, but the cited primary document does not establish an exact first-release year.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: Bell Laboratories Computing Science Research Center, Murray Hill, New Jersey.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: It generalized repeated ed-style editing into a non-interactive pass over input, useful for files too large to edit comfortably, complex edit scripts, and multiple global edits in one pass.

commands.name: tr
commands.description: tr translates or deletes individual characters in a byte or character stream. It has no concept of words or structured records.

anatomy.label: Input and output
anatomy.text: `tr` reads a character stream from standard input and writes the transformed stream to standard output; supply files with `< input` or connect a pipe.

anatomy.label: SET1` and `SET2
anatomy.text: Without `-d` or `-s`, characters in `SET1` map position by position to `SET2`. The sets are character lists, not regular expressions.

anatomy.label: Options
anatomy.text: `-d` deletes characters in `SET1`; `-s` squeezes repeated characters; `-c` complements `SET1`. Combined forms such as `-cd` are common.

anatomy.label: Portability and text
anatomy.text: Character ranges and classes depend on locale and implementation. GNU `tr` has limitations with multibyte UTF-8 text; use a Unicode-aware tool when characters may span multiple bytes.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Douglas McIlroy wrote the original Research Unix tr; the GNU Coreutils implementation is a later rewrite by Jim Meyering.

origins.label: When
origins.text: The command appeared in Research Unix Fourth Edition, released in November 1973.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: AT&T Bell Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: It made common character translation, deletion, and squeezing available as a small stream filter, so text cleanup could be composed with other Unix tools through pipes.

commands.name: wget
commands.description: wget retrieves a URL and normally saves the response under a filename derived from that URL. Check the scheme, host, redirect behavior, and destination before trusting or executing downloaded content.

anatomy.label: URL…
anatomy.text: Remote resources to retrieve. Check scheme, host, redirects, and the server’s policy before contacting it.

anatomy.label: -O FILE` and `-P DIR
anatomy.text: `-O` chooses an output file and may replace it; `-P` chooses a directory while keeping the URL-derived name. Ensure the parent directory exists.

anatomy.label: Recursive options
anatomy.text: `-r`, `--mirror`, `-l`, `--accept`, `--reject`, and `--domains` control crawling. Keep the starting path narrow, bound depth and rate, and respect access policy.

anatomy.label: Credentials and TLS
anatomy.text: Avoid passwords and session tokens in command lines. Keep certificate verification enabled; use a trusted CA file for an internal service rather than disabling validation.

origins.label: Creator(s)
origins.text: Hrvoje Nikšić wrote GNU Wget, with substantial later contributions from the free-software community.

origins.label: When
origins.text: Wget was publicly available by 1996; an archived November 1996 record identifies version 1.4.0 and Nikšić as its owner.

origins.label: Where
origins.text: The original project was hosted at the University Computing Centre in Zagreb, Croatia; the sources identify the host, not necessarily the place of coding.

origins.label: Why it emerged
origins.text: It retrieves files non-interactively over network protocols, supporting scripts, interrupted-download recovery, and recursive mirroring.

cases.what: Download one URL.

Check the host and destination before using downloaded data.

cases.title: Use Case 02: Choose a local filename
cases.what: Choose a local filename.
parts: `-O` sets the output path and replaces that file if it already exists; use a disposable or verified target.

cases.title: Use Case 03: Choose a destination directory
cases.what: Choose a destination directory.
parts: `-P` selects a directory while retaining the URL-derived filename.

cases.title: Use Case 04: Quiet download with explicit destination
cases.what: Quiet download with explicit destination.
parts: `-q` suppresses progress and most messages.
In automation, capture the exit status and log failures because quiet mode hides useful diagnostics.

cases.title: Use Case 05: Run a download in the background
cases.what: Run a download in the background.
parts: `-b` detaches the download and writes progress to wget-log.
Inspect that log and verify the output before using it.

cases.title: Use Case 06: Read URLs from a file
cases.what: Read URLs from a file.
parts: `-i` reads one URL per input line.
Review the list first because every entry can trigger a network request.

cases.title: Use Case 07: Resume a partial download
cases.what: Resume a partial download.
parts: `-c` requests continuation when the server supports it.
Confirm the remote object is unchanged before trusting a resumed file.

cases.title: Use Case 08: Limit transfer rate
cases.what: Limit transfer rate.
parts: The rate limit reduces bandwidth use; `200k` is approximately 200 kilobytes per second in GNU Wget notation.

cases.title: Use Case 09: Bound retries
cases.what: Bound retries.
parts: `-t 10` limits retries to ten attempts, avoiding an unbounded wait on a failing endpoint.

cases.title: Use Case 10: Download only when newer
cases.what: Download only when newer.
parts: `-N` uses server timestamps to avoid replacing a local copy unless the remote file is newer; timestamp support varies by server.

cases.title: Use Case 11: Mirror an authorized documentation area
cases.what: Mirror an authorized documentation area.
parts: Mirroring follows links and downloads page dependencies; `--wait=1` spaces requests.
Limit the starting path and confirm permission; Wget normally observes robots rules.

cases.title: Use Case 12: Limit recursive depth
cases.what: Limit recursive depth.
parts: `-r` follows links and `-l 3` caps traversal at three levels.
Review scope and site policy before crawling.

cases.title: Use Case 13: Constrain a recursive crawl to one host
cases.what: Constrain a recursive crawl to one host.
parts: `--domains` prevents following links to unrelated hosts, while `-l 2` and `--wait=1` bound depth and request pace.

cases.title: Use Case 14: Reject an unwanted file type
cases.what: Reject an unwanted file type.
parts: The reject pattern excludes GIF files during recursive retrieval; quoting keeps the shell from expanding it locally.

cases.title: Use Case 15: Accept selected PDF files
cases.what: Accept selected PDF files.
parts: The accept pattern filters recursive downloads to matching PDF names; bound the starting path and depth for a large site.

cases.title: Use Case 16: Authenticate without putting a password in shell history
cases.what: Authenticate without putting a password in shell history.
parts: Wget prompts for the password instead of embedding it in the command line.
Use HTTPS and avoid sharing the terminal transcript.

cases.title: Use Case 17: Authenticate to an FTP endpoint
cases.what: Authenticate to an FTP endpoint.
parts: Ordinary FTP does not encrypt credentials or content.
Prefer HTTPS or SFTP when available.

cases.title: Use Case 18: Trust an internal certificate authority
cases.what: Trust an internal certificate authority.
parts: Provide the issuing CA so TLS verification remains enabled.
Do not replace certificate validation with `--no-check-certificate`.

cases.title: Use Case 19: Identify the client transparently
cases.what: Identify the client transparently.
parts: A descriptive user-agent helps server logs identify the client; follow the service’s published request policy.

cases.title: Use Case 20: Send a non-secret request header
cases.what: Send a non-secret request header.
parts: `--header` adds an HTTP header.
Keep credentials out of literal command lines and use a protected credential mechanism when authentication is required.

cases.title: Use Case 21: Load a protected cookie jar
cases.what: Load a protected cookie jar.
parts: The cookie file can carry session authority.
Restrict its permissions, avoid logging it, and remove it when the session ends.

cases.title: Use Case 22: Force IPv4
cases.what: Force IPv4.
parts: `-4` restricts address selection to IPv4, useful for diagnosing a broken IPv6 path; it does not fix DNS or application failures.

cases.title: Use Case 23: Use an HTTP proxy
cases.what: Use an HTTP proxy.
parts: `-e` sets Wget configuration values for this invocation.
Use the proxy required by your network and avoid putting proxy credentials in the URL.

cases.title: Use Case 24: Check a URL without downloading its body
cases.what: Check a URL without downloading its body.
parts: `--spider` probes for availability without saving the resource.
Servers may handle HEAD requests differently from normal downloads.

cases.title: Use Case 25: Separate response headers from the body
cases.what: Separate response headers from the body.
parts: `--server-response` reports HTTP response headers to stderr; `-O -` sends the response body to stdout.
Treat that body as data, not trusted code.

cases.title: Use Case 26: Obtaining the Source Code
cases.what: Obtaining the Source Code.
parts: The URL is retrieved to a local file.
Verify the host, scheme, and downloaded content before executing or extracting it.
